1.	Was one Ephrem Renaud, of St. Eustache, Quebec, recently liberated on parole from the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary?
2.	If so, what was the length of his sentence, and how long was he detained in said penitentiary?

maintopic: QUESTIONS
speechtext: With reference to this question, Mr. Speaker, I notice that when it was called yesterday the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) took the attitude that it was not a proper question to ask, stating that it had not been the practice in the past for governments to reply to such questions. I would point out briefly, however, that this question of mine is quite different from questions or demands of a similar nature made in the past. The last occasion on which a question of this kind was asked in this house was on March 12, 1930, when the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Maophail) submitted a motion for a copy of all papers, letters, telegrams and other documents concerning a certain case of liberation. May I point out further that I am not asking for any confidential reports or documents; I merely wish to make certain of a group of facts where a certain person has been liberated-what was the length of his sentence, how long he had been detained, and so forth. These are facts; there is nothing in the nature of a demand for confidential reports. There is another point I would also make. When the Hon. Lucien Cannon, the predecessor of my good friend the present iSolicitor General (Mr. Dupre), refused to produce such documents, he made it very clear that he had examined the case, and he took the responsibility for refusing the production of those documents. In other words, someone must be responsible for cases of this kind. If the government does not desire to give to parliament information concerning cases of liberation, at least we should have a pronouncement from one of the ministers-and I think it should come from the Solicitor General-that he has looked into the matter and is quite satisfied that the case has been properly handled, and that for such reasons he does not desire to give the information. But the mere refusal to answer the question, without any acceptance of responsibility, is not, in my opinion, in conformity with responsible government. Someone must be responsible for any liberation on parole granted on the recommendation of the Solicitor General-

speechtext: Yesterday I made certain observations with respect to this question. This is a matter that touches, not the Solicitor General nor the Department of Justice, but the conduct of government. The question as to whether or not information of this character should be given is a question that has engaged the attention of successive administrations, and the rule has been not to furnish such information. And until the matter is properly debated and another conclusion has been arrived at, which would involve making known to the public every case that is dealt with-for one means all-the government does not propose to depart from that rule. May I point out that the responsibility is that of the government, because it is His Excellency the Governor General who acts upon the advice of his ministers. They accept the responsibility; it is provided by statute; and as one case means all, then until this house, by proper notice of motion and subsequent discussion and debate, has arrived at a conclusion other than that which I have indicated, the government, I repeat, does not propose to depart from the rule.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
I wish to speak in support of the amendment that was moved by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) and. I am led to do so because I cannot but believe that the Prime Minister, his colleagues and supporters are not yet fully seized of the facts in connection with the unfortunate condition in which the agriculturists of this Dominion find themselves at this time. I am led to the conclusion that the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in particular is unaware of the actual facts, and I am led to that conclusion because of statements that the right hon. gentleman has himself made and because of conclusions that he has drawn from the facts to which he referred in those statements. I am also led to the conclusion that that is the case because the government has not shown the same alacrity in dealing with the requests of the farmers as it has in dealing with the requests of other classes. Let me illustrate this by pointing out that when the manufacturers of barbed wire-and I presume they are not numerous-approached the government, the government was very quick to respond to their request and to fix a price for duty purposes on barbed wire, on the ground that barbed wire was being imported into Canada against the interests of the producers of barbed wire in this country. Precisely the same thing happened when the refiners of gasoline approached the government and again when the manufacturers of cars did so.
I have already, once in the house during this session, sought to enumerate the ills of the farmers in western Canada and I do not apologize for endeavouring to-day to repeat some of the statements that I then made. I do not hesitate, because of certain statements made recently by the Prime Minister himself. I remember that on one occasion the Prime Minister said in this house that hon. gentlemen opposite, referring to us on this side, had made statements that could not be substantiated. At the same time he said that we had made exaggerated statements as to conditions that prevailed in western Canada. He went further than that and said we had broadcast throughout the country statements that could not be substantiated in any manner

or form'. The right hon. gentleman did not enumerate the statements, but I imagine that he was: referring to statements that have been made on this side to the effect that many farmers in western Canada are insolvent. I believe I was one of the first offenders in that'..respect. I remember saying in my first address in this house, my maiden address on a. major debate, that I fully believed in my own constituency at least sixty per cent of the farmers were insolvent, and I repeat that statement to-day as being my honest conviction.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: May I ask hon. members to refrain from indulging in loud conversation while an hon. member is addressing the chair. In this building there are many offices provided for the transaction of business and also spacious lobbies.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
I should like to explain my understanding of the word "insolvent." I was using that word in the ordinary every day acceptance of the term. Who is the insolvent man? He is the man who is possessed of money, goods and land to a certain amount, and at any given date that amount is less than the total amount of his liabilities. That being the case, I affirm again that a large majority, in my opinion sixty per cent of the farmers in my constituency are to-day insolvent.
The Prime Minister, in refuting statements that we had made and in proof of his contention that they were exaggerated, made three major statements. In the first place he said that tens of thousands of farmers in the west had money in the bank. Then he said that new wealth to the extent of $1,900,000 had been produced in the west during the last three years. Finally he said there were a large number of cars in the western provinces and he suggested that the possession of those cars indicated that the statements we had made were exaggerated. I admit without any qualification whatsoever the truth of those three statements made by the Prime Minister; they are irrefutable. But I go further and say that they neither prove his contention nor disprove ours.
In the first place he said that tens of thousands of farmers had money in the bank. There is not the slightest doubt that that is true. But it is a very vague statement at best. There may be men who have a few dollars in the bank. There may be men who may have lots of money in the bank. There may be men who this spring obtained an advance from the bank, and then deposited the proceeds to their credit in the bank, and who

Agricultural Conditions
may now have a small amount which will be gradually diminishing during the summer. But if ever}' one of the tens of thousands of farmers that the right hon. gentleman speaks of have a large amount of money in the bank, our statements may yet be true.
May I draw attention to the fact that according to the census returns of 1926 there are in the three provinces that the right hon. gentleman mentioned 247,162 farmers. Taking my own statement that 60 per cent of these men are insolvent, what do we find? Sixty per cent of 247,162 is 148,000. That still leaves approximately 100,000 farmers who may have money in the bank. So I say again that the right hon. gentleman's statement to the effect that there are tens of thousands of farmers in the west who have money in the bank neither proves his contention nor disproves ours.
Then he said that since 1928, 81,900,000,000 of new wealth had been created in the west, and in addition there was S100,000,000 of new wealth created in the great mining areas in the three western provinces. That sounds like affluence, I admit. It sounds as though we were wealthy in the west. But I think it is advisable to analyze the statement and see what it produces.
The population of the three prairie provinces, according to the 1926 census returns, was 2,175,900. Very good. We find that the wealth produced per capita for the three years was $873.21 and the wealth produced per individual per annum, $291.07. The figure quoted by the right hon. gentleman was the gross agricultural wealth. It allowed absolutely nothing for the cost of producing that wealth. In the year 1928 it is very probable that the cost of production bore a reasonable ratio to the amount of wealth produced. In the year 1929 it was not so good, and in the year 1930 the cost of producing was greater than the value of the new wealth produced. I could produce all kinds of evidence to this house to show that such is the case, but I want to read a quotation from a letter that I received two or three days ago. It is a letter from a very reliable farmer who has been farming in our district for approximately thirty years, a man who takes no active part in politics, has no axe to grind, a hard-working man and a good farmer, with three sons to assist him in the operation of about nine hundred acres of land. This is what he says:	.
Well, I took my usual inventory and made up my books for the year on April 1st. My profit and loss account showed that the operations on the farm for 1930 were a loss of nearly $2,500.
He says further:
Still, we will try again. There are lots who say they won't. It is the first time in thirty years that I have farmed that I have seen the western farmers' morale so low.
I say to this house without fear of successful denial that the production of new wealth for another year or two more on that basis will certainly bankrupt the west. Close to the farm occupied by the writer of this letter, there is another farm of about nine hundred acres, farmed by four brothers, splendid men in every way, hard-working, intelligent, excellent farmers, with only one failing that I know of, and that is that they would never support me as a candidate for election. These men have assured me through a mutual friend that they made a loss on their operations last year. What is true of those two farmers is true of hundreds of thousands of farmers in western Canada. We do not want to go on producing wealth on the same conditions as those under which these men produced new wealth last year.
The right hon. the Prime Minister in his remarks said that we on this side of the house had stated that the western provinces were going into bankruptcy. He said it unintentionally, I think, but he did make that statement, as you will see if you look up Hansard. No speaker on this side of the house said that either of the provinces or all of them were likely to go into bankruptcy. We did not say that the whole of the farmers were going into bankruptcy. What we did say was that a reasonable proportion of them were.

That is probably what
the right hon. gentleman meant, and I accept his explanation that he was referring to the

farmers. But the grammatical construction of the sentence might suggest otherwise. At any rate, the words I have quoted are the words that he used. We were referring in our statements on this side of the house to only approximately sixty per cent of the farmers. In this connection I would like to make a suggestion. The Bankruptcy Act of this Dominion provides a means whereby business men who are hopelessly entangled and harassed beyond all possibility of getting out of their financial difficulties may go into bankruptcy. I would like to see a simplification of the procedure under the Bankruptcy Act, to have certain amendments made which, with proper safeguards against fraud, would make it possible for a farmer who is hopelessly involved to avail himself of the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act. That is a suggestion which I think might be considered by the government.
The next statement which the right hon. the Prime Minister made is also irrefutable, namely, that there is a large number of cars in western Canada-261,778 in the three prairie provinces, to be exact. I know that the right hon. gentleman merely stated a fact. I do not believe that he intended any implication, but I gathered from the response that his statement met with from his followers, that there was a certain implication in the minds of many of them. It is rather remarkable that since I have been here in the east I have had on several occasions the suggestion made to me that the farmers of the west have been very extravagant. It has been suggested that they have bought too many cars and other things, like radios. There is one thought that comes to my mind in that connection. Who is more entitled to own a car than the farmer? Who can use a car more profitably than the farmer? The car has not only been a very profitable thing for the farmer to have, but I will tell you what it has done for the farmers' wives of the western prairies. It has made life far brighter for the women of the prairies and for the children. Before the advent of the car it was a rare experience for the hard-working wife of the hard-working farmer to have an outing. Many a farmer, having worked the whole day, and working six days a week, puts his horses away at night. Perhaps on Sunday he would hitch up his team and take his wife and children to church. That was about the limit of the outings the wife and children had. In these days things are different and the car is used to give a little pleasure to farmers' wives and children. I fear there is a

misconception in the minds of a great many people regarding the statement made concerning cars owned by farmers. When I was going home for the Easter recess I travelled for a short distance with a very delightful old lady. She told me she had heard there were a great many members of parliament on board the train and after a while she asked me if I was one. I did not like to deny it, although in a great many cases I find the fact is not appreciated. She told me she had a good friend in the House of Commons but did not say on which side of the house her friend sat. I hope however the hon. gentleman is on the other side of the house. My reason for saying that is that presently she said to me, "Is it not a f'\ct that your farmers in western Canada 1 ^ve built large houses, own cars and radios?" I said, "Madam, undoubtedly it is true that a few of our farmers have large houses, but more of them dwell in shacks or very poor houses. It is a fact that many of them have radios, and I think they are entitled to them." To me it is passing strange that the men who derive their wealth from the producers of wheat own cars without comment. On the other hand the man who produces the wheat must not own a car.

In case of a possible
misunderstanding I will repeat what I said. I did not for one minute accuse the Prime Minister of endeavouring to reflect upon the farmers. I said that there was an idea prevailing, or something to that effect, that the farmers were not entitled to own cars. I repeat that statement.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
The right hon. gentleman told of the number of cars in western Canada. In the previous paragraph of his speech he will find he was referring to farmers. I would point out that in the three prairie provinces 34 per cent of the people are urban dwellers and 66 per cent are dwellers in rural districts. The automobiles to which my right hon. friend referred have not all been purchased by the farmers of western Canada. In case the right hon. gentleman states that I am positively accusing him of making that statement, I will say at this time that he did' not make it. He said that the people of western Canada purchased these cars, and I am pointing out to him that 34 per cent of those people live in villages, towns and cities and 66 per cent in the rural districts. I venture to suggest that if a survey were made as to the ownership of those cars it would reveal a reversal of the figures I have stated. I suggest that 66 per cent of the car value in the western provinces would be credited to city, town and village dwellers. The average man in the city, town or village owns a good car, and nobody would blame him for doing so. The farmer usually buys a cheap car, and very often a second hand one discarded by the city dweller.
My right hon. friend made three suggestions as to why it was time hon. members on this side of the house ceased criticism. I wish to make my statement carefully, because I might be misunderstood. First he wanted to know how we could expect the banks to continue to lend money if we continued to talk in the way we have been talking. Mr. Speaker, I venture to opine that no bank will grant fewer loans because of statements made by hon. members in this corner of the house, and no bank will grant more loans because of what has been said by hon. members opposite. In the past when I have wanted loans, as now
and again, I do, I have found that the banker took me into his inner sanctum and put me through a drilling. He wanted to know what I owned, how much was free from encumbrance and asked a great many other questions to learn whether or not I would be a proper risk. That is the practice of banks everywhere. I will go further and state that the 60 per cent of the people in my constituency to whom I have referred could not get bank credit anyway. Therefore they are not prejudiced by the fact that I have made a statement in connection with the matter. In the second place the right hon. gentleman stated a gentleman had said to him, "We must uphold the credit of Canada." I believe that. He said a certain gentleman had written to him and said that somebody should be prevented from speaking because agreements of sale were being offered and could not be sold. May I say in reply that hon. members in this comer of the house were not sent here to assist in the disposal of agreements of sale. We were sent here for a specific purpose. Having acquainted ourselves with the conditions in our respective constituencies we were sent here to make those conditions known to the house. Having made discoveries as to what was needed for the good of Canada it is our duty to make our desires known. Mr. Speaker, I consider that to be our duty. Again I will explain that the Prime Minister did not intend to imply that we should moderate our speech. Certainly not; he does not do it himself.

Mr. Speaker, I shall bring my remarks to a conclusion by saying that I believe I have fulfilled the duty imposed upon me when I was sent here to represent to the best of my ability the constituency of Last Mountain. I have made statements which can be substantiated, and I have not made one statement which cannot be substantiated.
Agricultural Conditions

Before I close however I would like to state frankly that I do not believe the government is responsible for existing conditions; I believe they are not wholly responsible. I believe I made that statement before. Probably they did something to aggravate the situation during the last session of parliament but on the other hand I think there are things they may do which will relieve the present situation. I do not believe however that it is within the power of the government to cure the present economic situation. However we ask them only to do the best they can. With regard to the last paragraph of the amendment moved 'by the hon member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) I think there are suggestions therein contained which the government might well reconsider.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree very largely with what has been said by the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Butcher) with respect to agricultural conditions in western Canada. I believe practically every hon. member from western Canada, regardless of his seat in the house, will agree with him. However, I do not purpose at any great length to take up the time of the house in a discussion of the subject matter of the amendment because I feel such action would be merely a repetition of the five weeks' debate on the address. However I would like to place on record some of the activities of the group in this section of the house with respect to the issues involved. Knowing the serious plight of western agriculture I must admit I have some sympathy with the amendment.
However, I do feel constrained to comment upon the fact that for many years we in this corner of the house have been bringing forward measures for the relief of agriculture. Generally we have found our Liberal friends opposing and voting them down. But now that they have been transferred to the opposition benches they have suddenly become reformers. Of course, I am not objecting to that, I am not criticizing them for it; on the contrary I welcome even this belated action on their part. As an illustration of what I mean, may I deal with the demand made on the government on Tuesday last by the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan). He demanded that the government set a maximum rate of interest of 6 per cent on farmers' liabilities. I quite agree with him that something like that must be done. But I would remind him that in 1923 when the Bank Act was up for revision this group moved an amendment that would have had the effect of setting a maximum rate of 7 per

cent for bank interest. Of course, that limitation is already in the Bank Act, but the bankers have been able to override it by technicalities. The amendment that we introduced would have made it impossible for them to do so. What' was the result? Every member on the government side of the house -the Liberal party at that time-voted against it, along with the Conservatives who then sat on this side of the house; and I have no doubt that my hon. friend from South Huron, being a good party man, would have done the same had he been here. Of course, he was not in the house at that time, and we cannot tell what he would have done, but I can hardly conceive of him breaking with his party. I do not like to cross swords, with my hon. friend because, as I appreciate, he is a "bonny fighter" in the interests of agriculturists.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman has no right to make such an implication.

There is nothing to take back. I think my hon. friend would be the first to admit that he is a good party man, and that is all I said about him. I have never heard him deny that. I am not questioning his integrity or his ability as a member of parliament.
Now, sir, I come to the amendment itself, and I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) on the very able case he made out and his effective presentation of it. The moving of an amendment to a motion to go into supply is a very dramatic and spectacular way of placing a case before the country. Generally, I do not condemn the practice; under certain circumstances I would do it myself. We in this corner of the house have done it, but we have never done it except on issues that we had been fighting for previously and with respect to which we found we could not get action any other way. But there are circumstances in which this course is positively damaging to the very cause supposed to be served. It must not be assumed that because our Liberal friends moved this amendment they are the only members concerned in the issues involved. From the very moment of the opening of this session we in this section of the house have been dealing with all the issues mentioned in the amendment and in the speech of the hon. member who moved it. The only difference is that our work was not done in a spectacular way. We were not looking for publicity, w? were looking for results.

Agricultural Conditions

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN

I do not wish to suggest that our hon. friends merely want publicity.
I assume they are perfectly honest and perfectly sincere in their action. I am criticizing their methods not their motives.
Now. let me take the question of freight rates dealt with by the mover of the amendment. I may say that since we came to Ottawa we have had frequent conferences with the ministry and we have been in constant communication with the United Farmer bodies back in the country. To show what is being done in this regard, may I read, in part, a letter addressed to us by Mr. Frank Eliason, secretary of the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section? This is only one of many letters that we have received from that body since the opening of the session. The letter is from Saskatoon under date of April 29, 1931, and, in part, reads:
As a result of our negotiations and representations in connection with freight rates on canned goods, we have gained a certain amount of experience and we have come to the conclusion that what is needed in western Canada, at this time, is a freight association,-an association which will be composed of representatives from the United Farmers of the three western provinces, of the boards of trade for the three provinces and of the wholesale and retail distributors of the three provinces.
George H. Smith, our provincial government traffic expert, returned last night from Alberta where he has received unanimous support for the proposal. We have also been in touch with the United Farmers of Manitoba and have their support. Mr. Smith is going to Manitoba this week in an endeavour to line up the wholesalers and the distributors. The first meeting, which is called for the purpose of forming the organization, will be held in the parliament buildings, Regina, on May 1st. We have decided to discuss four points. First: the advisability of forming a western Canada freight association, which association shall deal with freight rates only. Second; present freight rates on canned goods from the east. Third; present freight rates on canned goods from the west. Fourth; rate construction of the Canadian National Railways capital.
At future meetings Hudson's Bay rates, mountain rates will be discussed, also the adjustment of local freight rates as compared with through rates.
Now. with particular reference to the question of the disparity between domestic and export freight rates on grain, I may say that the group in this section of the house have had the matter under consideration for a long time. On April 23 we addressed a letter to the three prairie premiers. It is signed by myself and was written on the instructions of this group. It reads as follows:
I have been instructed by the independent groups here to suggest that the three prairie governments make an application to the railway commission for an equitable adjustment between domestic and export freight rates on grain.
We would appreciate it very much if you would discuss this matter with the other prairie premiers-

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
Don't leave us out of the
freight rates.	.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
We	are not. It will
rest with the prairie premiers, and if possible they will take that into consideration when they are dealing with it. However, if we secure a reduction it will work for the benefit of British Columbia the same as for the prairie provinces. I will proceed with my letter:
We would appreciate it very much if you would discuss this matter with the other prairie premiers and we trust that action will be taken without delay. We have thoroughly canvassed the situation here and find that there is nothing directly that we can do and this would appear to be the only proper procedure in order to get results. I do not need to discuss the point at issue as the matter has been before the public for a long time.
This letter was addressed to the Hon. J. E. Brownlee, premier of Alberta; the Hon. J. T. M. Anderson, premier of Saskatchewan; and the Hon. John Bracken, premier of Manitoba. Under date of April 28 Mr. Bracken wrote us from Winnipeg as follows:
I wish to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 23rd instant, in which you suggest that the three prairie governments make an application to the railway commission for an equitable adjustment between domestic and export freight rates on grain. I will be very glad to have the matter considered at the next conference, which I expect will take place within the next two weeks.
Mr. Anderson wrote us from Regina under date of April 29, as follows:
I am in receipt of your letter of April 23rd, and in reply may say that consideration will be given to this matter.
We are not yet in receipt of a reply from the premier of Alberta. We might have saved ourselves a lot of effort and trouble if we had moved an amendment such as is now before the house, but I think every member knows that such a course would have been barren of results.
With regard to the fiscal policy of the government, the proper time to consider and discuss it is when the budget comes down. Then we will have that policy in detail and will be
Agricultural Conditions

able to discuss it in detail. Then, too, we can, and undoubtedly will, move an appropriate amendment expressing our counter policy. That, it seems to me, is the time to discuss it instead of taking up the time of the house now, when it is merely an academic question, and when we do not know exactly what the government will do.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
Why waste time
now?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
My hon. friends have
been wasting time; I am pointing out the uselessness of this discussion. Now, sir, with regard to the general agricultural conditions, may I say that committees representing this group have waited on the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture since the beginning of the session and have made representations to them, discussing the situation with them; and we have in return received some assurance. We have not got all that we asked for, but we know that something is being done in the prairies. We know that the three prairie governments are administering the necessary relief in the way of seed grain aDd so forth and that they have the financial backing of the federal government.
Take again the question of the processing of meats and marketing of live stock, referred to in the amendment. My hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) came to Ottawa this year with some well thought out and clear cut suggestions regarding these matters. Committees representing this group have waited on the Minister of Agriculture at least four or five times and have thoroughly discussed the whole situation with him. The minister received us sympathetically, and we know that he is going into the matter. So far as we are aware, nothing definite has been done yet, but we do hope that as a result of our negotiations some action will be taken.
Take again the duty on farm implements repairs. Last year the government raised the duty on repairs from 6 per cent to 25 per cent. There are millions of dollars' worth of American-made machinery on the farms of western Canada and no doubt a great deal of it on the farms of eastern Canada as well.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
What government was
that?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
This government; and I may say that the imposition of this duty would have imposed serious hardship upon those farmers. Representations were made to the Prime Minister on the floor of the house from this section last year and in response he delayed the imposition of these duties for

one year. The duties come into effect on the 1st of July or August of this year. But we are not sleeping at the switch; we have our eye on that. We know that no branch factories have been built in Canada by such concerns as the J. I. Case company and the John Deere Plow Company, and the farmers will be penalized if the extra duty is put on. We have already made representations to the Prime Minister. We did not wait to move an amendment; and while, as I say, we have no assurance, we hope that something will be done at the appropriate time. If nothing is done with respect to this and other matters, then we will take the proper course. But I believe that in the meantime we have taken the right course. While our Liberal friends were deliberating the moving of this amendment, we were steadily working on and considering these problems. I believe that what we have done is the proper thing to have done, and I do not think that any good and useful purpose will be served by moving an amendment. In fact, I believe that is the best way of hindering governmental action while matters at issue are still under consideration. I do believe, however, that before this debate concludes we are entitled to some statement from the government, and I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) that he avail himself of this opportunity to make his maiden speech and to tell the house what he has told our committee when we have discussed the subject with him privately. He may not have carried it out to fruition yet, but I am sure the house would welcome a statement from him as to what he has under consideration with respect to the matters we have discussed with him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
I
will not take up more than a few minutes of the time of the house. I had been, and still am, in some doubt as to how to vote on the amendment. Provided I was assured it was what is known as a straight vote of want of confidence in the government, I would vote against it, because, elected as an independent, I would consider it my duty to give the government a run for their money, so to speak, allowing them an opportunity to develop their policies before voting against them. On the occasions when I voted against the late government on a motion of want of confidence, or what was technically such, it was always on questions involving such a distinct and definite line of policy concerning matters which were of such importance, either to British Columbia or to the industries I represent, as to compel me to view

Agricultural Conditions
it in the light of immediate necessities rather than from the point of view of the consequences to the government.
As regards the amendment now before us, I find fault with it as being somewhat vague in its terms. It condemns the government for failing to announce any agricultural policy to the house. That is somewhat indefinite. And later on it suggests emergency measures to meet the present crisis-that also is indefinite-and to make adequate provision for the processing of meats, the marketing of live stock and so on. I am always ready, if I find fault with something the government are doing, to suggest an alternative policy and one which I am prepared to support, because I do not believe in condemning the government simply for the reason that they have not done something which neither I nor anybody else can do. Perhaps I should be best advised to follow the attitude of my hon. friends to my left a few weeks ago and refrain from voting, in spite of the obloquy which apparently attaches to such an action, which however was quite within the rights of those hon. gentlemen, although we do not know how long they will enjoy the privilege.
What I rise for particularly at this time is to put on record, as typical of many others, some representations I have recently received from the district I represent. One of them has reference to a matter I discussed in the debate on the address, and the other arises out of the remarks of the Prime Minister some weeks ago with regard to the wealth of the people of western Canada as indicated by the number of motor cars, etcetera, owned by the farmers. I will not enter into any argument with the Prime Minister along the lines taken by my hon. friend from Last Mountain (Mr. Butcher), but I would say this. As regards what appears to be the enormous sum of money invested in cars, that is a very old method of making out an ex parte case; it is simply putting large issues against small ones. For instance, suppose the government introduced legislation to collect in taxation from the people of Canada the sum of one hundred thousand dollars, and suppose I went to a man in the street to whom one hundred dollars was a large sum-a man who perhaps never possessed a thousand dollars in his life. Suppose I said to this man, "Listen to this, Bill: they are going to take one hundred thousand dollars away from you people." That would make a considerable impression upon him. He would compare it by his standard of one hundred dollars a month in wages and he would say to himself, "One hundred thousand dollars! Why, that is an awful sum they are going to 22110-86
take away from the people." He does not know, nor can he be expected to know, that it represents, on the basis of our present population, something like one cent per capita. But that is the way specious arguments are advanced. Now, it would be more appropriate, in discussing the question of motor cars, if the question were asked:	How
many of these cars were bought in the last six months or year, and how many have been paid for? To go back a number of years is not to make a fair comparison.
Here is a letter which I wish to put on record, a letter I received to-day from a man in the west. It is addressed to myself and reads:
Having read press notices of the efforts of certain western members to draw attention to the serious conditions prevalent in their constituencies, to which the Prime Minister and his cohorts persist in turning a deaf ear, I presume upon our slight acquaintance to address you in this connection.
While the Hon. R. B. Bennett and his confrere, Mr. Manion, may deem it fitting to minimize the growing seriousness of conditions, let me assure you that we here are in a position to know that the western members have been guilty of no exaggeration. The Conservative press, of course, make a feature of Mr. Bennett's loud-mouthed condemnation of "blue ruin" speakers, hut such an attitude as bis is simply a refusal to look facts in the face. The country now realizes how empty were the promises to "end unemployment." to "blast our way into the markets of the world," etc., etc. Unemployment is now a great deal worse than when this government took office, and the bottom is not yet reached.
The hon. Mr. Bennett speaks of the farmers on the prairies, but apparently forgets there are 600.000 people west of the Rocky mountains. Mr. Bennett was to expand our export markt-, but since the election half of the coast lumber business has closed down, and most of the balance is running on part time. One firm, normally employing about 800 men, is shut up tight, with no prospect of reopening and very few of the men laid off have found work or have any prospect of doing so. This condition has been repeated over and over. I have word of one very large mill, running six hours per day. five days per week, with a base wage for labour of 18 cents per hour. Ask Mr. Bennett to multiply that up. subtract living expenses, and see how many automobiles he can buy. Most of the loggers now out in camp are making barely enough for board, with not enough margin to buy clothes and pay their fare to camp and back. As you know, this work is very seasonable and when the men get back to town there will be nothing for them but begging on the street.
It is within my own personal knowledge that that statement is absolutely correct. I know that the firm to which he alludes, ordinarily employing nearly a thousand men, has been shut down. It is a common salutation for the men in the woods to say to each other, "Have you earned your board to-day?"
ItEVISED EDITION
Agricultural Conditions

Many have been put on a piecework basis and sometimes they are unable to earn even their board. The letter continues:
Less than half the canneries will be running this year, and none will pack late fish-
That is, those running in the fall-
-so the fishermen will have no money next winter. The copper mines and pulp mills are all running with reduced crews or not at all.
The Coast Copper Company Limited, operating in my district, a subsidiary of the Consolidated Mining & Smelting Company of Canada Limited, which has been running for about fifteen years and employing a comparatively large crew, has shut down with no probability of soon reopening. The letter continues :
Notwithstanding Mr. Bennett's promise to help the dairymen, the farmers are getting still lower prices for their produce, and are paying almost as much for feed as when wheat was selling for $1.50 per bushel. Probably the grain dealers and holders of Canadian Pacific Railway stock are buying automobiles, but the dairymen are not. Consider the poultrymen with eggs bringing them eleven cents per dozen. The one consoling thought is that very few of us will be paying Doctor Tolmie's one per cent tax.
The writer becomes sarcastic at this point. That is a tax commonly referred to as "Tolmie's tag day," which is put on all incomes above $25 per week for married men or $15 per week for single men. It is collected weekly so that a stenographer earning $60 per month for one or two months and then being idle the rest of the year would still have the privilege of paying an income tax. One week's work, one income tax. The letter continues :
Let me repeat the warning of Mr. J. S. Woodsworth, that conditions are certainly such as to induce rioting and serious disorders before another year. To-day I was talking to a man who has been prominent in the business life of Vancouver for many years, and he admitted that the present outlook was much less promising than it was six months ago.
To-night I cut two clippings from to-day's issue of the Daily Province. I enclose these to you, as illustrating the difference between fancy and fact, the cartoon showing what the Conservative press would have people believe and the advertisement showing conditions as they are. And this is the first day of May, in this west of seasonable occupation when, if ever, employment should be available!
This cartoon, familiar to all, appeared in the daily press. It depicts the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) with two clubs in his hands, one marked "sound logic" and the other marked "proven facts." He is shown chastising two so-called calamity howlers and putting them to rout. The headline reads: "Would anyone else like to tell me that Can-

ada is ruined?" That is the cartoon referred to. The advertisement to which he refers appeared in the Daily Province under the heading "Help Wanted Male"-rather a travesty on the heading. It reads as follows: Revelstoke
No men need come to Revelstoke looking for work.
500 men have been waiting here six weeks for )obs on Canadian Pacific railway.
There are also some 300 local men unemployed.
Hundreds of men are arriving daily who cannot be fed nor employed.
City Clerk,
Revelstoke. B.C.
That is not an advertisement published by some union during strike time, but was got up and paid for by the city of Revelstoke in an endeavour to keep unemployed men away from that place so that the city would not be faced with the burden of keeping them. As the writer of the letter which I have just read, mentioned, these conditions existed at the beginning of May, which should be almost the most favourable employment period in British Columbia. A few days ago I saw another advertisement along the same lines published by the city of Trail, warning unemployed men to keep away from that vicinity.
The other communication is in the form of a post card evidently circulated among a large number of dairymen and farmers to be signed and forwarded to their parliamentary representatives. No doubt other hon. members from British Columbia will be receiving these post cards. It reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
Due to the great deflation in the prices of all agricultural commodities it is absolutely essential to the existence of the industry in the Fraser valley and Vancouver island that costs pf production be greatly reduced. The greatest factor in production costs is the price of feed grains and a very large proportion of feed grain prices is freight. The Canadian farmers in this area are paying as much for freight per ton on Canadian grown feed as do farmers in Japan for the same article delivered to them.
May I say in parenthesis that it is not the same article; that sent to Japan is of much higher value being No. 1 or No. 2 wheat, and that delivered to British Columbia, at $4.20 per ton extra freight, is No. 5 or No. 6 wheat. The post card continues:
This situation is serious and calls for action by the government pursuant to our repeated demands.
As a farmer, resident in your constituency I request you to insist upon definite action being taken immediately by the government in accordance with our petition made to it, to remedy this obvious injustice by ordering the immediate cancellation of freight differentials on feed grains coming to this district.

Agricultural Conditions
The post card obviously should have read "coming to this province." This refers to a matter I brought up while speaking on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and on previous occasions, the discrimination between the export rate on wheat going foreign from Vancouver and the same or lower grades of wheat coming to British Columbia for domestic use. I brought this matter up the other day and I explained the situation to the house. This matter has been through the regular procedure of being brought up before the Board of Railway Commissioners and once, if not twice, it has been referred to the privy council of Canada, which is the government. The matter rests there now and has been resting for something like fifteen months. I urged then, and I urge now that this is the best time to take action in this matter. It is something tangible, it is something which would really help; it has not the vagueness of a general condemnation of the government. I am not condemning the government, I asked it to take prompt action on a grievance which has been repeatedly brought before this house and the government. I am always faced with the reply: "Oh, this is not the occasion on which to announce a policy." A statement upon going into supply on agricultural estimates should offer a very appropriate ocoasion to announce such a policy because if it is left until we are in committee we would oe restricted to particular items. As it is not .ikely there will be an item referring to this .natter, it will be difficult to debate the subject. Unless the government is prepared to take immediate action by means of an order in council, which would be preferable, it should announce its policy now.
To go back to my remarks in connection with labour conditions, I omitted to urge the necessity of this government having a conference with the provinces before the close of this present session. Should that not be done, how can money be voted for relief for this coming winter? Just as surely as the sun will rise to-morrow morning, much relief will be needed this coming winter. I urge that a conference be held at an early date to enable the government to take appropriate action at this session. I may add it will be of no use to enact legislation similar to that passed during the session of last September because most of the municipalities are broke and will not be able to finance a fifty-fifty proposition. They strained their resources last year in the hope that only temporary relief was needed, and they will not be able to continue payments this year.
In closing I would again impress upon the government the necessity of an announcement as to its policy with regard to railway rates, and the need of an immediate conference with the provinces with regard to unemployment relief.
Mr. CAMERON R. McINTOSH (North Battleford): In associating myself with the want of confidence motion which was moved by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown), I take it that this motion and the debate on it deal entirely or almost so with the Department of Agriculture and the minister who is at the head of that department. It is important that everything pertaining to the question of agriculture be brought forward during the present session and as early as possible. I believe it is unnecessary to state that the condition of this primary industry in western Canada is not good; it is absolutely unsatisfactory. Therefore it behooves all members from western Canada and also from many other	parts	of	the	Dominion,
especially those who represent agricultural ridings, to see that the existing condition of affairs is brought before the house and the country.
I do not want to say anything derogatory in connection with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir).	There	is	a feeling thatperhaps he has been unduly criticized. I do not think that is	the case	and	I do notbelieve that is the	feeling	on	this	side of the
house. We do not want to criticize unduly any member of the government. What we want to do, though, is to draw the attention of parliament and the Canadian people to what I said were serious conditions in the agricultural industry from coast to coast. I do not really see why the Minister of Agriculture should be overly criticized. Perhaps there is one reason why, and I shall touch on it later.
So far as I understand, he is a native-born Canadian; he was born in one of the best parts of Canada, in western Ontario, and I do not see any reason why he should apologize for that. The other day the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan) mentioned the fact that the minister was a product of Huron county. There is no better county in Canada. There are many splendid counties and districts in central Canada, eastern Canada and western Canada, any one of which no person need be ashamed to say was his birthplace. So the criticism cannot be on account of the portion of Canada in which the Minister first saw the light of day, or on account of his ancestry, or on account of his
Agricultural Conditions

iducational training; because he went through the primary and secondary schools as well as one of the leading universities of Canada. He has educational training and I am proud that a minister of agriculture with that training was selected for Canada. Training of that kind means developed ability, and I hope that ability in a practical way will be shown later by the minister not only on behalf of the agricultural industry but also as applied to the questions of government that will come before him.
Moreover, the minister moved west and was one of those who took part in the opening up of that vast empire of western Canada. He has done his duty there, not only educationally but in an agricultural way. He represents a splendid riding in this house, and he also fills an important position. It is on account of none of these things that any criticism has been levelled at him to-day. Therefore it must be for some other reason. May I ask what that reason is, Mr. Speaker? The other reason I would say is the political company he is keeping, the party with which he is lined up, the policies with which he is identified, not only in this chamber, not only in western Canada, but all across this land. So I would say that westerners are counting on the minister to take definite action although he is part and parcel of an inactive cabinet and government-action, again I say, although he is identified with policies which I think are absolutely too restrictive and are not going to bring prosperity to Canada-yes action, because I think the only tariff policy that will mean anything to this country, that will build up all portions of it, is a compromise tariff policy, a fair, moderate fiscal policy. When you resort to extremes, I care not what party be in power, you cannot make the machinery work; you are only going to turn back the hands of time so far as Canada is concerned, and instead of prosperity bring rhe opposite condition of affairs which we certainly now have.
Might I say a word about the question of secession? I think it was the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) who brought up in the House of Commons the question of secession. I notice he got some big black headlines in the daily press of Canada, and I was surprised to find that we have in this country a section of the daily press floundering around and trying to make some propaganda out of a question that does not in reality exist. There is no systematic secession sentiment in Western Canada any more than there is in Ontario or Quebec or the

marilimes. The hon. member said that references made to that question in times gone by had been regarded lightly, but we should not regard lightly the references that are now being made to secession; we Should be very much concerned about them. He said also at the United Farmers of Alberta convention in Calgary he rose and voiced his sentiments against secession. Further on he drew attention to the distressed and discouraged people who might try anything-that is, they might resort to secession in order to bring redress. He wound up with this expression of thought: that if this session of parliament will not do something towards relieving agriculture of the extra tariff burden imposed on it, we shall have to face the disintegration of our Dominion.
Those are serious words, serious sentiments; they are echoes of a fiscal problem that come well within the sphere of . debating. This afternoon I want to give the house and the country the sentiments in my own riding with regard to secession. There is absolutely none. Before I left for Ottawa I went through my riding and held eleven or twelve important meetings. At the end of each meeting those who were in attendance-and often there were three or four hundred present- were given an opportunity of their own free will and accord to bring up any resolution, and this afternoon before I resume my seat I shall read some of the resolutions that were proposed. You will not find among those resolutions one on secession. There was not in any of the meetings that I addressed in my riding one iota of secession sentiment.

speechtext:
There were in the hon.
member's own province.

I shall deal with that

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: The hon. member had better hurry up.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
There is no need for
hurry. If what I have said be true in the riding of North Battleford, it is practically true in Saskatchewan. It is true that here and there we have an odd sentiment with regard to secession, but as I said, there is no connected movement with regard to secession. Wherever you get in any part of Saskatchewan or western Canada any sentiment in regard to secession, what does it signify? It signifies merely a reaction to the administration which now holds office, and which my hon. friend supports by advocating a conservative self-supporting economic dependent

Agricultural Conditions
Canada, a reaction to their fiscal policies, and to what they have done to Canada since the election took place on July 28. That is all In other words, the men and women of western Canada are protesting resolutely and continuously and will continue to protest with regarded to the fiscal policies with which this government has saddled Canada and which are causing the people of the west to see not a ray of hope in the future.
Beyond this any suggestion that has been made has emanated from a source unconnected with any recognized organization or movement. There is therefore no secession sentiment in western Canada-none in Saskatchewan. none whatsoever in the riding of North Battleford. That we have a government in power that is not satisfactory to western Canada; that its policies are out of joint as compared with the policies we ought to have in this country, faced as we are at the present time with very serious problems, is no reason why we should have word go all over Canada through the daily press to the effect that there was a concerted movement towards secession in western Canada. This talk about secession sentiment is all nonsense; it is not worth paying very much attention to. I thought I would draw the attention of the house to it because I am from western Canada, and I know western Canada as well as I know the east, and I know the east as well as I know the west, and I am not afraid to stand up here and tell what I know to be the facts about that question.
Let me now come to the promises that were made during the election by hon. gentlemen now members of the government, with regard to agriculture, because it is the question of agriculture that is now before the house. They said that they would protect agriculture, would foster and develop agriculture. They said they would bring about the stabilization of economic conditions and the continuity of trade, freedom from the manipulation of tariffs at home and abroad. They said that they would find a foreign market for our products. Have they done so? Have they protected agriculture? Have they fostered and developed it? Have they brought about the stabilization of economic conditions? Have they brought about continuity of t.rade? Have we been free from the manipulation of tariffs at home and abroad? Have we? Have they found a foreign market for our products? To all these questions I would answer, no.
In the special session last September what did they do with regard to agriculture? Well, they increased the tariff on 170 articles which the farmer and labouring men of this country
must buy. We put up tariff barriers on all these products, and when we did that, we did something which helped to put the farmers in the condition in which they find themselves to-day. I have a letter here bearing on what is taking place in that regard, but before reading it let me say that last September we raised the tariff on the following articles:
Cultivators, harrows, seed-drills, horse-rakes, horse-hoes, seufflers, manure spreaders, garden seeders, weeders, and complete parts of all the foregoing.
Ploughs; farm, field, lawn or garden rollers; soil packers; complete parts of all the foregoing.
Mowing machines, harvesters, either selfbinding or without binders, binding attachments, reapers, harvesters in combination with threshing machine separators including the motive power incorporated therein, and complete parts of all the foregoing.
Hay loaders, hay tedders, potato planters, potato diggers, fodder or feed cutters, ensilage cutters, grain crushers and grain or hay grinders for farm purposes only, post hole diggers, snaths, stumping machine and all other agricultural implements or agricultural machinery, n.o.p., and complete parts of all the foregoing.
Scythes, sickles or reaping hooks, hay or straw knives, edging knives, hoes, pronged forks, rakes, n.o.p.
We raised the tariff on all those agricultural implements. Under the Liberal tariff before the special session, the tariffs on all these implements of production were 7i, 7i, 6 and 20 per cent. These rates were all raised under the general tariff to 25 per cent. Sometimes it is said that the tariff increases that were made in the special session have not meant any increased price for those who were buying these implements. Let me quote from a letter I have received which bears on that very point. It says:
While there is no advance in prices, there are very few declines. What we are iooking for is cheaper goods, and while some of the papers are protesting that the retail trade are not lowering their prices, the fault as I see it is with certain manufacturers. Steel is very much cheaper than a year ago; still steel goods do not come down to us.

Out in western Canada
it is cheaper because there is limited industrial labour to perform. The letter continues :
Copper was quoted a few weeks ago as being the cheapest for thirty-five years; still copper goods are very little less. You will admit that Mr. Bennett promised that goods would not go higher but he never said anything about going lower, and it is on that that the manufacturers are working.
Agricultural Conditions

That is the interpretation put upon the increases in the tariff by the people in all portions of western Canada, and I would say that the tariff increases have helped to accentuate the serious conditions which are to-day obtaining in the agricultural industry. It was no wonder, then, that when parliament assembled at the present session we moved an amendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
When the friends of my
hon. friend were in power, did they reduce the cost of agricultural implements to the farmers in western Canada through their tariff reductions?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: Yes, they reduced them, and more than that, they brought about in this country conditions of prosperity so great that the farmer never thought that he was paying too much for anything.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has
not answered the question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
It is an old question
which has been answered time and again.
I was referring, when I was interrupted, to the amendment that we brought down to the address. We were told when parliament assembled that the government would consider measures to ameliorate present conditions. Those conditions are not ameliorated, and they show no sign of amelioration. The people of Canada are becoming disgusted with present conditions, and there is no sign whatever of improvement. So I say that that promise in the speech from the throne is not worth the ink it is written with. The speech from the throne also promised to bring about . prosperity hitherto unattained. Well, the government have not made any move to bring such about. Canada is not prosperous to-day. The government said they would make it prosperous, but they have not done so. Further, the government promised to furnish safeguards against the recurrence of like depressions in days to come. More than that; the government were going to explore the origins of the agricultural depression. They were going to set out on an exploration policy. I am wondering whether they have yet completed that exploration policy. What have they explored, and what have they discovered? They were going to explore the conditions from which we are now suffering in a domestic sense.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: "Exploration" must have been a misprint for "exploitation."

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
My hon. friend suggests that the trouble with Canada is in the sphere

of exploitation, and the inference is that the present government has helped to put Canada in her present exploited condition. Those were some of the promises that were made by the government. There has been nothing explored and nothing discovered. No safeguards have been provided against a recurrence of the depression. The depression, in fact, is worse to-day than it was before. Prosperity has not come, and there is no amelioration of conditions. These are facts.
The government also promised to provide for an orderly marketing of the wheat crop, and further intervention, if necessary, because of changing conditions in world markets. There was to be a reduction in the costs of production and marketing of the wheat crop; more stable markets were to be provided, and satisfactory returns received by the grain growers. Well, we are selling a certain amount of wheat, but look at the price we are getting for it. The price bears no comparison to what we are paying for all the industrial products that we need on the farms and in the homes of western Canada, and which we must have just the same as any other part of Canada. The big spread between the price that the farmer and the labouring man receives for his product and the price he has to pay for the things he has to buy is the discouraging feature of present conditions, and until the western farmers and labourers see that gap closed they are not going to be satisfied that this government is doing anything for either agriculture or labour.
More than that. Mr. Speaker, we have an amendment moved by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown), in which we are told that the agricultural policy of the government has not been brought down, that markets have not been found for our goods, and that consequently something must be done if Canada is to be brought back to prosperity. If, Mr. Speaker, the policy of the Department of Agriculture has not been brought down- at least the government say that is the fact- the sooner it is brought down the better, because in this want of confidence amendment I believe there is dynamite enough to move any government.
