speechtext:
We have had nothing
but hearsay. The onus of propounding a policy is on hon. gentlemen opposite, not on the opposition.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: It was on my hon. friend for eight years.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: Yes, eight years of prosperity. And until my hon. friends do bring down their policy we will bombard them and force them to bring it before the house and the country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
What did my hon. friend
do for the past nine years?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
And that is not all.
Some further points come into this want of confidence picture. I must say it appears to be "some" picture, when one looks at it for a while. We say the policies of the government tend to restriction rather than to expansion; that is true. Canada's trade is decreasing by millions and millions of dollars, month after month and year after year; we will soon have no foreign trade at all-or no trade outside of Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: Blue ruin.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
And all because the
policy of the present government "blue-ruin" like, is to have Canadians live unto themselves, to make our people believe they are prosperous when they are not, and to attempt to build the country up fiscally and commercially by pulling at our boot straps.
Another question faces the government in this amendment, and it is this: If our international trade goes to pieces; agriculture will become more and more paralyzed. It is becoming more and more paralyzed every day and every week.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: More blue ruin.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
And that is why we are
calling upon the government to take cognizance of its blue ruin consequences in this country, and asking it to do something.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: What about the past government?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: Will the hon. member permit a question?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
No, not just now. In
the closing paragraph of the amendment we find the expression, "emergency measures to meet the present agricultural prices." These emergency measures are requested because wheat marketing has not been successful, and other agricultural products are not bringing satisfactory prices in the markets of the world. To all these representations on the part of the
opposition up to the present time the government has suggested nothing in the way of an agricultural policy. I do not wish to make any statements of a disparaging character concerning the Minister of Agriculture. I do not know him intimately, but I have a very high regard for him. I would say, however, that the minister has made one mistake: he has over-sold himself to this country, in an agricultural way. That is more reason than ever, Mr. Speaker, why the minister or some other hon. member of the government should come forward and announce the government's agricultural policy all along the line, thereby letting us know exactly what they have in mind to cure conditions. Up to the present time they have done nothing. That is a serious statement to make, but it is made in connection with a serious condition of affairs.
I have before me a statement contained in the press of western Canada concerning a speech of the Prime Minister.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: The Star-Phoenix?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
It was in my own paper, The News, and it at least tells the truth. This is a press despatch sent from Ottawa to western Canada with regard to the seven points mentioned by the Prime Minister when he spoke in this house regarding western conditions:
1. No government of which Mr. Bennett is the head will consent to any policy of pegging the price of wheat.
That is correct, is it?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: Sure.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
All right. Western
farmers say: The only reason we want to peg the price of wheat as an emergency measure is that the government pegged the price of 170 industrial articles, and it should therefore peg the price of wheat.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: Yes, that is the reason. Therefore Mr. Speaker it is needless for hon. gentlemen opposite to make a row. The government started the practice of pricefixing. and they are afraid to go through with it. That is all. I think the farmers are dealing absolutely fairly with the government; all they want is for this government to come through and do for the farmers what they did for the industrialists.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
They will come
through; don't worry.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
Then, we come to statement No. 2:
The three prairie provinces are not experiencing undue hard times.
Agricultural Conditions

Is that true? That is what he said. Then we come to No. 3:
Nothing approaching an acute depression or an economic crisis exists.
The Prime Minister said that. Then No.
4 is as follows:
Cases of hardship and actual want are confined to a few isolated individuals.
That is No. 4. Now, will hon. members listen to No. 5-
An hon MEMBER: Five loaves and two small fishes.
Mr. MeINTOSH: It is as follows-no five or two about it.
Tens of thousands of prairie farmers have substantial bank accounts.
By the time I am through perhaps hon. members will know they have not. Then No. 6 is as follows:
Three hundred millions of dollars invested in automobiles and tractors in the prairie provinces bespeaks their solvency and economic well-being.
That is a ringer. Then No. 7:
Prevailing impressions that western Canada has been hard hit are due, entirely, to exaggerated statement of Liberal, Progressive, Labour and Independent politicians, who have been guilty of decrying their country for purposes of party politics.
I want to refute that statement, and all the other statements I have read. I have before me the result of an investigation carried out by Doctor William Allen of the university of Saskatchewan with regard to two well-defined agricultural areas in western Canada. One area which Doctor Allen, as an expert, investigated in an agricultural way was the provincial riding of Kindersley. The other area investigated was the provincial riding of Turtleford. That provincial riding is part of the federal constituency I represent in the House of Commons. The provincial riding of Kindersley is part of the federal riding represented in this house by the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael). Doctor Allen confined his investigations to two of the main areas in western Canada. I might say however that the conditions he found in those two portiov.3 would be representative of other parts of the west, because one area is in the north and the other is towards the south. Doctor Allen found the following:
.... that the average farmer debt in Kindersley county is $4,084, and in the Turtle-ford district. $2,262, both sums taking into account debt-free farms.

Let us do a little calculating with these figures. Provincially speaking, if we add the S4,0S4 for the Kindersley electoral district to the $2,262 for the Turtleford electoral district wc get a total of $6,346. Dividing that figure by the figure 2 we get an average of $3,173. that is the average debt of all the farmers in those two important areas in Saskatchewan. If we take that average and multiply it by 250,000, the number of farms in western Canada, we have a total indebtedness of western farmers amounting to $793,250,000. That says nothing about the share the farmer has in municipal debts, provincial debts, railway debts, urban debts and federal debts. It says nothing about the millions of wealth brought into western Canada by settlers from different parts of the w-orld; it says nothing about the $5,000,000,000 of wheat values that were produced in western Canada and shipped eastward to build up the.Dominion as a whole. When we think of that prodigious debt, and when we realize that these are facts disclosed by investigation in regard to only two areas in western Canada, we must conclude that agriculture is not in a very satisfactory or sound condition. I would not go so far as to say that western Canada is bankrupt; I do not think it is. But I do say the farmers must be given a real opportunity to go forward, that their debts must be cut down as far as possible, that they must be encouraged to make the best of their surroundings. In order to do that there must be a government in power to encourage the farmer by a fiscal policy adapted to his needs, to encourage him by strong governmental leadership, the leadership of men of vision, statesmanship and power. Such a government will appeal to the people of western Canada. I do not believe the present government has done as much in that direction as it might. I do hope that in the months to come there will be a change of heart on the part of the government in regard to its support of agriculture and the encouragement of that industry, and that by bringing down a constructive and forwardlooking policy it will improve the condition of the western farmer. If this is done I have no objection to this government getting credit for it. It is not a question of party politics, it is a question of the well-being of western Canada and the whole Dominion.
With regard to these distressing conditions, may I enumerate to the house a number of resolutions that I have received passed by the farmers of the North Battleford federal district at the meetings to which I have referred. These resolutions were passed volun-

Agricultural Conditions
tarily, the farmers were not asked to pass them. I think these resolutions indicate truly the conditions of agriculture in the area I represent in this house and also that they are fairly applicable to the entire west. All these resolutions ask for action on the part of the Prime Minister, action on the part of the Minister of Agriculture, action on the part of the Conservative rank and file all across the Dominion. Resolution No. 1 asks:
For government supervision of the grain exchange.
Number 2:
That the government guarantee a minimum fixed price of 70 cents per bushel, basis No. 1 northern. Fort William or Port Arthur, for the 1930 wheat crop.
The farmers are not asking for these things without knowing full well why they are asking for them. Number 3:
That the government take over the supervision of the banks with regard to interest charges, and bring about their reduction to a maximum of 7 per cent.
Number 4:
That the government declare a moratorium until such time as conditions affecting agriculture shall sufficiently improve to warrant its removal.
Number 5:
That the government set a price on all wheat used for consumption in Canada of $1.25 ner bushel, and the price of flour per 98 pound sack be set at a reasonable price not exceeding present prices.
Number 6:
That all freight rates be lowered 20 per cent.	.
Number 7.
That all interest and indemnities on taxes be cancelled until a fair measure of prosperity is restored.
Number 8:
That all debts owing banks, machine companies. and wealthy corporations by farmers be cancelled till a fair degree of prosperity is restored.
Number 9:
That all banks, natural resources, timber, mines, oil wells, water-powers, be nationalized.
Number 10:
That extension of credit should be through the banks alone, controlled by the government, with a suitable provision made for those in distress.
Number 11:
That in view of the privileged position of industries other than agriculture, government assure cost of wheat production at $1 per bushel.
Number 12:
That the government be asked to set up a board of standards to maintain _ a proper relationship between the price the farmer has to pay for commodities that he has to buy and the price he receives for commodities which he has to sell.
Number 13:
That the legal rate of interest of 7 per cent as set out in the Bank Act be enforced.
The source of all these resolutions, Mr. Speaker, is to be found in the fiscal policy sponsored by hon. gentlemen opposite. For instance, on February 18, 1931, at a meeting held at St. Walburg the following resolution was passed unanimously:
That this meeting go on record as being in favour of freer trade in lieu of protection as practiced by the Bennett administration.
There, as I say, Mr. Speaker, you have the source of all these resolutions, they are all concerned with the fiscal policy of the present administration. All these resolutions have grown out of the high tariff policy of this government, out of the increased tariff rates passed at the special session, out of the increased tariff rates the government are expected to put into operation at the present session; in a word, these resolutions arise out of the artificial fiscal policy of the government of the day, and until that policy is very much modified I am satisfied the people of western Canada will not feel happy and contented. It is not a question of secession. It is a question of the people of western Canada'recognizing that the policy of the present government is not the policy for western Canada. They are strongly of the opinion that there must be a change, and that the next government that takes office must recognize in its policy the interests not only of one section, but of all sections of the country; it must introduce a fiscal policy that will bring about the development of Canada as a whole. In no other way will Canada prosper and reach her full development. Until something in that direction is attempted, I believe conditions in western Canada will not improve very much.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, to put on Hansard a few of the resolutions passed by the local lodges of the United Farmers of western Canada, and also by wheat pool committees. I believe the people behind these resolutions are entitled to recognition. They are fighting the battle for fiscal freedom in western Canada, and they are doing their best to call the attention of the whole Dominion to the conditions which now prevail in the prairie
Agricultural Conditions

provinces. Here is a resolution passed by the Cavalier local lodge of the United Farmers of Canada on December 10, 1930:
That we advocate government supervision of the grain exchange.
That we ask the federal government to guarantee a minimum fixed price of 70 cents for the 1930 wheat crop.
The rural municipality of Mervin passed unanimously the following resolution on December 6, 1930:
Resolved that the Dominion government be requested to set a minimum price for wheat, of 70 cents per bushel basis No. 1 northern, Fort William or Port Arthur.
The next resolution that I am reading was passed by the wheat pool "Speers local" on December 6, 1930.
In view of the very serious situation that has developed as a result of the collapse of the wheat market:
We the members of the wheat pool, "Speers local" urgently request that the Dominion government guarantee a minimum price of 70 cents a bushel at Fort William for No. 1 northern wheat grown during the season of 1930.
That was moved by R. Miner and seconded by S. Cunningham.
The council of the rural municipality of Round Hill passed the following resolution on December 20, 1930:
Resolved: That this council demand that Dominion government take steps to stabilize wheat market so that minimum price of at least 70 cents be maintained.
I have a resolution passed by the Edam local of the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section, covering practically the same ground. Then there is a resolution from Spiritwood covering a little more ground. But since I have not the time to read these and the other resolutions under my hand, I should certainly like to have them on Hansard for the information of the house and of the country. Not only should I like to put all these resolutions on Hansard, but I should also like to give their source and the names of their movers and seconders.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I hope the present government will bring down its agricultural policies and its budget as soon as possible in order that members on this side of the house may see whether the government as a whole is looking up or down; whether it intends to go forward or backward; whether it intends to make progressive history for Canada or the opposite; whether it intends to recognize the ills of agriculture in western Canada or to turn a deaf ear to those ills, as it has done since it assumed office. May I say-

has expired.
[Mr. McIntosh [

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
I have just a word to say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker. Let me say to the government that I hope it will not follow the downward course; that is-
Not down, down, down to the uttermost down,
For the pathway is long and deep;
And as you go down to the uttermost down, "iour're prone to get fearful and weak.
But up, up, up to the uppermost up

Oh, the pathway is steep and long-
And as you go up to that uppermost up, Cheer all the way with a song.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the present debate, and I should be neglecting my duty as a representative of my constituency if I did not speak to the amendment which has been proposed. I believe the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) was induced to move this amendment by the speech delivered in this house, -by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. During that debate I heard Liberal members on this side of the house, one after another, representing to the government the conditions as they had found them in western Canada, and I believe that every one of them was telling of the conditions exactly as he had found them in his own constituency. And when they were through the Prime Minister got up and began to read them a curtain lecture. He told us that we on this side were only playing politics, making such speeches only for political purposes. I resent a statement of that kind. If, having entered politics, I am not to be allowed bo get up and tell the truth regarding conditions, then the sooner I get out of politics the better. But let me tell the government, Mr. Speaker, that I do not intend to be bullied either by the Prime Minister or by anyone else. The Prime Minister may be able to bully his own cabinet and to keep their mouths shut, but he will not keep our mouths shut on this side of the house. He will not prevent us from portraying conditions as we find them, no matter how much he may curtain-lecture the house and attempt to bully us. We will not be bullied. It is contrary to my nature anyway.
No man in the history of Canada, Mr. Speaker, has done more to discredit public men in the eyes of the common people of this country than the Prime Minister. He went from coast to coast during the last election, preaching prosperity, promising to usher in better times, and representing the conditions in the country as something for which the

Agricultural Conditions
then Liberal government was responsible. He said to the people, "Put me in power and I will give you heaven and earth-everything; I will give you whatever you want. You shall have (prosperity; there will be good times." Well, the people took him at his word and returned him to power. And what do rve find now? We find harder times than we have ever known. The result is that the common people have the impression that no public man can be relied upon. They say, "There is the Prime Minister. He made promises which he knew quite well he could not carry out." He was a high pressure salesman all right; he sold himself to the country. He went from coast to coast with his propaganda and sold himself. Let me say that if any stock salesman had gone from coast to coast as he did and had sold stocks, making representations such as he made, that stock salesman would be in jail to-day. They would have had him arrested. The right hon. gentleman had mo regard for what he promised. He went up the high mountain, showed the Canadian people the glories of the world, and said, "You can have it all if you only vote for me." And they voted for him. But they have learned their lesson; make no mistake about that. The people in western Canada have learned their lesson and now they know they were handed a gold brick. The conditions as hon. members on this side have indicated them are the conditions as they exist in the west, and it is because those conditions are as they have been represented that I now get up to speak on this amendment.
When the Prime Minister was speaking in Calgary on June 19 last year, he said, "We will look over the top of the hill and beyond the horizon to make provision for the Canadian agriculturist." I do not know whether he has ever got up on that hill. That was the hill of prosperity which he was going to have the Canadian people climb. Well, we have not even got to the foothills yet.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: You never will.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
We never shall with this government; you are absolutely right. Let me tell hon. gentlemen opposite that they are going in the wrong direction. They are not reading the signposts along the road. They are going into the valley of despair. The Prime Minister, after he was elected, said, "Wait until the special session; I will pass resolutions, I will vote $20,000,000, there will be prosperity." When the special session came he said, "I was wrong; wait until we have the regular session." And now that the -egular session is in progress, what does he say? He says, "If I am given health and
strength I will bring you prosperity." Why, Mr. Speaker, we are filled with such promises. We want action. We have had too many promises; we want some of the action which the right hon. gentleman was going to give us. But we are getting none of it. We are, as I say, going deeper and deeper into the valley of despair, because hon. gentlemen opposite are not observing the signs along the road. They are going the wrong way. I advise those hon. gentlemen to turn around and go in the other direction if they want to get anywhere. Their whole policy is wrong, and this country will get nowhere under such a policy.	.
I wish for a moment or two to refer to two or three things the Prime Minister said in regard to conditions in the west. Speaking in this house, he said:
Wherever men have had regard for economic laws and have kept free from speculation and wild dreams of sudden wealth, they are happy and contented and have provided a good livelihood for themselves and their families.
And he went on:
What is the cause of the great depression in western Canada? Hon. gentlemen opposite know that the most important cause is speculation.
What does the Prime Minister mean by speculation? That is an important thing. If he means speculating in grain or speculating on the stock exchange, I want to tell him that I know thousands and thousands of people in the west who never invested a dollar in either of these forms of speculation, and yet they are in despair and in financial difficulties at the present time. I know thousands of them. I know that some of the best men are suffering, although they have never invested a dollar in speculation in their lives. But if the right hon. gentleman means by speculation the investment in land and farm machinery, in horses and equipment of various kinds, then I will admit at once that a good many farmers have speculated. There is no doubt about that. But let me tell the Prime Minister that farming conditions in the west have Changed considerably within the last thirty years. I nave been farming there for that length of time, and when I went there I found a piece of land of 160 acres a good-sized farm. But farms have expanded. The farmers, like the manufacturers, have gone into mass production, and we know that to-day 640 acres constitutes an ordinarysized farm. A man can farm 640 acres today as easily as he could 160 acres thirty years ago. There has been a considerable increase in the use of farm machinery and equipment generally, and great strides have been made in the mode of farming. Conse-
Agricultural Conditions

quently, farmers can take up more land. If that is speculation, all right, but does the Prime Minister intend to condemn a man because he has confidence in the country, because he believes ;n it, because he has investigated it and is satisfied with the result? Surely not. Surely the right hon. gentleman is not going to condemn a man because he says: This country is all right and I am going to buy more land, I am going to buy belter equipment, I am going to build a better home and a better barn. Surely the farmer has the same right to do that as has the manufacturer to erect a bigger plant, to put in better machinery and to go into mass production. That is all the farmer has done, but the Prime Minister gets up and dares to condemn him foi his action. It ill becomes the Prime Minister or anyone else to condemn the farmer for doing these things; he is to be commended rather than condemned.
The Prime Minister then went on to say that during the last twelve months the banks had increased their agricultural credits by 16 per cent. I will agree with that statement, but I am surprised that the increase was not greater. In the spring we borrow a little money with which to seed our land; in the fall wo borrow a little more to harvest our crops, and after the harvest is over we pay our loans and start off with a clear sheet, or, if necessary', borrow a little more. But what were the conditions last year?	After we
harvested our crops we could not pay any loans, and I guarantee that ninety-five per cent of the present outstanding loans are simply renewals of old notes. With the exception of a new credit here or there, this increase is made up of renewals, and I am surprised that the figure is not much greater than that given by the Prime Minister.
Conditions are serious in western Canada. 1 have lived there for some thirty years and I have never known them to be worse than they are at the present time. I have seen the farmer wiped out with frost, with drought, with hail, but always he would say: Next year things will be all right. We do not find that spirit to-day; the note of optimism has gone. We are sowing our crops but we do not know what we will reap. Should we obtain a good crop, we figure that prices probably will be bad and we will be worse off than ever. One thing which this government should do is to restore that spirit of optimism which has always prevailed in western Canada.
I would like to read one or two letters which I have received from my constituents. One received from Hodgeville reads as follows:
Times here are terrible. The farmers are in a state of panic not knowing what to do.

They cannot start seeding as we have had no rain and the soil is drifting and blowing so that some days one can scarcely see ten feet away. On top of this adding another mortgage for seed and feed, and many for food supplies.
I have never seen such despondency' and discouragement among the masses, even the hitherto well-to-do. God only knows how it will all end.
The next is a letter received from a clergyman, reading in part as follows:
This has been the most discouraging spring I have seen in the w'est and I have been here for twenty-one years norv.
He is a clergyman giving his independent view. Another letter reads as follows:
If the people of eastern Canada wanted to aggravate the people of the w'est to the verge of war and bloodshed they couldn't have found another man in all the world with a disposition more suitable to carry out such a program.
The writer refers to the present Prime Minister. The letter continues:
Talk al>out a bull in a china shop causing trouble-if he could do more damage than this bird at Ottawa he would need to be a superbull. _	'
I don't suppose there is another man in the Dominion of Canada or any other country that could have caused so much trouble and suffering and discontent in such a short time in office
The writer of this letter is a good Tory who has always voted against me. The letter continues:
And his last speech at Ottawa ought to convince the farmers of the west w'hat they can expect from the federal government in the way of relief from their present difficulties.
Another thing our Conservative supporters ought to know by now, and that is out of eight members they sent from Saskatchewan to Ottawa, two proved to be feebleminded

I wonder who they can be?
-and the other six w'ere deaf and dumb. So I must say to the people of Saskatchew'an. why spend $32,000 to keep these birds at Ottawa when they could be kept so much cheaper in Saskatchewan ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
If the hon. minister
will name the two hon. members to whom I have been offensive, I will withdraw my remark.

Agricultural Conditions

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
The hon. member is
simply making it worse; he is making it offensive to all the hon. members.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
I will withdraw the
statement, but I might say that it was made in a published letter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: Even so, it is not parliamentary.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
This letter was published in the press of Saskatchewan. I will withdraw that particular statement, but will continue with the letter. It is as follows:
But on the other hand if the farmers of the west have such substantial bank accounts as our beloved friend, Mr. Bennett, says they have, why should they worry about a few thousand dollars more or less, or whether they keep their feebleminded at Ottawa or Weyburu.
1 Now. in regard to our provincial government, Premier Anderson needn't try to bolster up the Bennett government for it can't be done. Mr. Bennett's last speech at Ottawa swept away the last thread of confidence that the people of western Canada had put in this so-called super-man and left bare his true character-that of a rank imposter.
Premier Anderson said there never was a government in power before that gave as much money to the west as the Bennett government, but he didn't say that there never was a government in power before that took so much money from the west. This Bennett tariff wall has cost the people of the west around $50,000,000. Then he tries to make a big man of himself by giving the west a few million for their unemployed and the rest goes to the eastern manufacturers. This is the kind of a square deal the west is getting from the Bennett government.
If the people of western Canada are going to submit to this particular brand of British fair play then I must say they haven't got any more backbone than a jellyfish.
That letter was written by Mr. Tom Clark of Willows, Saskatchewan, and is dated April 27, 1931. This man is credited with having voted against me in the last election, and has always voted Tory. His letter gives his opinion of the present government.

speechtext:
I would gladly do so, but I am afraid they would be unparliamentary. I ask here and now: what does the
present government intend to do? What is their policy with regard to agriculture? We have sat here and listened and every one of us has asked: what is the government's policy with regard to agriculture? Farmers are writing to me from day to day and week to week to this effect: "Keep after the government and try to make them tell us what they intend to do for us. We have been endeavouring to do that, but we get no answer." The government seems to be deaf and dumb, just as this man said.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), however, did bring out a policy to which some hon. members on this side have referred. This announcement of policy, which appeared in MacLean's magazine, is called Canada's new agricultural policy, and it is divided into twelve heads:
1.	A national marketing board.
That is all right.
2.	Lower costs of production obtained by increased yield per acre.
That is a nice thing.
3.	Sowing of land to crops best suited to it.
That is all right so far as it goes.
4.	Research work to discover fertilizer required for different soils.
That is all right too.
5.	Immediate survey of seed grain, seed vegetables and fodder crops.
Those are all right. Then we come to number 6, and I want the house to pay particular attention to this:
6.	Creation of "bull clubs."
Then the seventh:
7.	Immediate improvement of quality of swine.
8.	Eradication of disease among poultry.
9.	Research work on feeds.
10.	Increased effort to eliminate parasites.
11.	Transformation of experimental farms into local educationl centres.
12.	Cooperation with provincial governments in carrying out policies.
Those are all right so far as they go, but practically every one of them bis been in operation for years and they are not going to help our conditions one bit. I can answer all of them just the same as many questions are answered in the house. I can say that numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 are all answered by number 6. Then number 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 and 12 are all answered by number 6 too, and that is the "bull clubs." That is all there is to it; there is nothing in it to help the farmer at all. It is all window dressing, all show, all froth, eyewash. We want something substantial. We want something that is going
Agricultural Conditions

to do some of us some good. This is of no use at all. The .people of western Canada are in a desperate state, and desperate conditions require desperate measures. We are asking the government for desperate measures, something that is going to bring us out of the woods, but we are getting nothing. The government are deaf and dumb.
Of course we know the Prime Minister came out to western Canada and at Regina said that the thing to do was to go into mixed farming. He said: We are going to get a revolving fund of $5,000,000 and bring you out on the Minnesota plan. This fund of $5,000,000 is alright; we will take the money quickly enough, but what the western farmer is looking for to-day is not a chance to get further into debt but a chance to get out of delbt. It is all very well to bring in the Minnesota plan when prices of live stock are rising, but it is a different proposition when they are declining as they are at the present time. I would say to anyone who is thinking of investing money in a scheme of this kind: take a long last look at your money, because it is going to be many a day before you see it again; kiss it good-bye when you put it into the fund, because I doubt if you will ever see it again. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mullins) seems to favour mixed farming. There appears, however, to be a wrong impression about mixed farming. A year ago the price of butter was away up, but now domestic butter is worth about ten or twelve cents a .pound and eggs are worth eight or ten cents a dozen. We do not hear so much about the price of beef, but I have before me the report of the Dominion Live Stock branch, markets intelligence service, giving the top prices at Edmonton for the week ending April 2, this year and last year, as follows:
1931	1930
Butcher steers	$5 25	$10 50Select bacon hogs	6 85	12 10
So that present prices are just about one-half of last year's prices. If the farmers can make money at .the present starvation prices, then last year they must have made a fortune, and I doubt very much whether the farmers to-day can make money with prices of farm produce as they are.
But there seems to be a wrong impression altogether as to mixed farming conditions in western Canada, and I wish to say just a word or two about this question. In my opinion western Canada can be divided into three great areas. There is one area which, on account of climatic and soil conditions, is fit only for ranching. There are some dis-

tricts in the southern and eastern parts of Alberta and the southern and western parts of Saskatchewan, and other districts here and there, which on account of the soil-sandy, stony, gravelly, or rough-or on account of climatic conditions-extent of rainfall-are fit only for ranching. Then there is the broad open prairie, which, on account of climatic conditions, is fit only for grain; we can grow grain; we cannot raise live stock. We are not sure of rainfall from day to day and week to week so as to get pasturage for the stock. We are not sure of water for watering the stock. If we had plenty of water, the proposition would be different, but I have known of farmers hauling drinking water twelve miles, and one cannot raise live stock if one has to haul water that distance. Many of these farmers do not keep horses for farming; they use tractors entirely. We can grow small grains and wheat, but we cannot grow oats or flax. It does not take as much rainfall to grow wheat or flax or some of the coarser grains. It does not pay us to go into mixed farming. Here and there, throughout that district, wherever it pays us to go into mixed farming, we do so; we have some stock. Then there is the great northern part which has its rainfall, its water, its shelter for the stock. It is fitted for mixed farming, but the people there are already engaged in mixed farming. It may be possible that some of them should go into it a little further, but any farmer who goes into mixed farming must do so gradually. Let him buy one or two head of stock, go into the thing gradually, and find out how to handle stock. Do not let him rush into it wildly and think he is going to make a fortune, because it cannot be- done. Let him handle just what stock he can handle properly and no more. One thing is sure; he cannot make a fortune out of it at present prices.
What our farmers are demanding now from the Prime Minister is that he make good his election promises. He promised to find a market for our wheat and other farm produce at better prices. The Conservatives went through my constituency and promised that if returned to power wheat would be selling at $1.80 and $1.90 a bushel. Put the Conservative government in, they said, and wheat will go up from eight to ten cents a bushel right away. Some of them even guaranteed that if the Conservative government came into power wheat would go up within two weeks by ten cents a bushel. As a matter of fact, wheat went down ten cents a bushel during the first five days this government was in power. It has been going down ever since, and the bottom is not in sight.

Agricultural Conditions
The Prime Minister says that we are now selling wheat. No, Mr. Speaker, we are not selling our wheat; we are giving it away. To sell a commodity at 50 or 60 cents a bushel is quite different from selling it at $1.50 or $1.60 a bushel. At the time the Liberal government was in power the price of wheat was around $1.50 a bushel, but since this government took office the price has been from 50 cents up to less than $1 per bushel. Why does the government not do something with regard to the price of wheat? They are doing nothing; not a man on the government benches has a word to say about it; they are deaf and dumb still. What the farmers of Saskatchewan are demanding is that the government do something, that they sell our wheat, that they look after our farm products, because our western farmers cannot continue very long to raise crops under the present conditions.
The present policy of the Conservative government is absolutely wrong. It is absurd to put a wall around the country, shutting out all foreign goods; it simply means that we cannot buy from anybody and therefore we cannot, sell our goods. There is not enough gold in the w'orld to use as a purchasing medium; the only way we can sell our goods is to take other goods in exchange, and unless we take other goods in exchange ' for our wheat we cannot sell it at a profit. Therefore I say that to put a wall around this country, preventing us from exchanging our wheat for the goods of other countries, is the wrong policy. Where we should be to-day is not at the London conference, but at the Briand conference, among the wheat buyers of Europe. I do not think anything worse could have happened for the wheat growers of western Canada than what happened at Rome. Our High Commissioner in London went there, and what did he do? There were the buyers and there were the sellers, and he split them into two different camps. Who does the seller want to make friends with? With other sellers or with the buyers? Any man who is selling commodities knows that the seller wants to make friends with the buyers. But our High Commissioner split this conference of European buyers and European sellers into two, and he said:	The sellers will all
meet in London for a conference, and you buyers can meet in France three days before that conference. Nothing worse could have happened for the wheat growers of western Canada than to divide the conference into two camps in that way. We as sellers do not care what the other sellers think. The ones wo are interested in are the buyers. They
are the people we want to make friends with; they are the people we should be doing something for in order that we may be able to sell our products to them.
The policy of the Liberal government, Mr. Speaker, has been altogether different from the policy of this government. The policy of the Liberal government was for wider markets, more open markets, freer trade. It was to take the goods of other countries in exchange for our goods, to make treaties with other countries, to get preferences in their markets and to give preferences in ours. We believe that if the Liberal government were in power in this country to-day and the Dunning budget were in force, we would have no trouble in selling our wheat at a good profit. That is the policy that we have always advocated and it is the policy we advocate to-day. The policy of this government, on the contrary, is to build a wall around the country, and for the country to live within itself. The countries of the world that have followed that policy in the past now realize that they were wrong and are beginning to tear down their walls, while Canada is beginning to go in the opposite direction. It is building up a wall just as other countries are beginning to tear theirs down. All over the world today the tendency is towards freer trade and more open markets.
I want to make this suggestion to the government: What we should have at the present time is a wheat board to market our grain.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: Why didn't you have it When you were in power?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: The price of wheat was so high then that we did not need it. But to-day, since this government has closed all the markets of the world to our products, we do need it. If we are going to market our grain, it is absolutely necessary that we should have our grain under some single control, even if it be under the farmers' control, such as the 100 per cent wheat pool. Either that, or it must be under government control-one or the other. You cannot enter into arrangements to market grain when you have none to market. How can the government go over to England and talk about marketing grain when it has no grain to market? You can no more do that than you can market overalls or lobsters when you haven't got any.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: The government has lots of lobsters.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
Yes, and some are boiled and some are raw. There must be a single control, and the best way to bring that
Agricultural Conditions

about, I suggest, is through a wheat board. Establish a wheat board and give it control, with power to investigate conditions and make arrangements for disposing of our wheat. Give it power to enter into quota arrangements, for a premium, if necessary.
I wish to refer to the proposal that I made in the house the other night with regard to fixing a price of wheat for home consumption, and to answer a few objections to that proposal. There was an idea that it would be a terrible thing for the consumers in Canada. If you look at the price in Canada to-day, you will see that one cent's worth of wheat goes into a pound loaf of bread, with wheat at 60 cents a bushel. With wheat at $1.50 a bushel, you would be putting only 2 cents' worth more of wheat into a loaf of bread; it would be increasing the price of a loaf of bread to the consumer in Canada by about 2 cents, and that would not mean much to the consumer. What does the report into the alleged combine in the bread-baking industry in Canada say in this connection? It points out that the price of wheat has very little to do with the price of bread. It says, at page 12:
The difference in flour prices, which are the medium through which the influence of wheat makes itself felt, does not account, then, for the difference in the two levels of bread prices, the one in 1913 and the other in the years 1925-1930. ... In other words, even if the baker had got his flour for nothing in 1930 he would still have charged 5-1 cents a pound for his bread; in 1913 he would have charged only 2-3 cents.
No, Mr. Speaker, the price of wheat has very little to do with the price of bread. It is the prices of the other ingredients and the costs of distribution that are the big factors in the price of bread. Fixing a price for home consumption would not interfere in any way with the millers. Our millers who are milling for export would still receive their wheat to mill into flour for export at export prices. So if we set a price for home consumption it would not interfere with the millers.
Another objection was this, that if we fix the price for home consumption in Canada, the western farmers would go into the growing of wheat wholesale. I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that at 70 cents a bushel it does not pay the farmer to grow wheat; it would pay him only part of his expense, and he would still be losing money. So that if the farmer received a price, say from 70 to 73 cents, which would partly pay his expenses, he would not be induced to go into the raising of wheat on a wholesale basis.
rMr. Donnelly.!
I want to hurry on because my time has about expired. It is necessary that the spirit of optimism in western Canada be restored. Nothing would do more towards its restoration than to have the price of bread and flour fixed for home consumption. The farmers of western Canada would then feel that the people in the east are behind them, and trying to help them, and the support of this part of the country would help to buoy them up under the present difficult conditions. It would not mean very much to eastern Canada, but would do much towards the restoration of the spirit of optimism among the western farmers. I say the government could not consider anything better than to take some action of that kind. I repeat my suggestion that the government appoint a wheat board, and I ask them to investigate the proposal of fixing the price of wheat for home consumption in order that the wheat growers of western Canada may receive the benefit.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I wish first to take this opportunity of thanking hon. gentlemen opposite-perhaps they did not intend it any too kindly-for the great pains they have taken to bring before this house and before the people and the press the fact that I am inexperienced. They have said that I am "green." That is true. There is not in this house a member greener in politics than I am-and God grant that I may remain so. They have also referred to my limitations in various resipects, agricultural and otherwise; in this also they are correct. In confirmation of their statements, I wish to say that on those points we agree in every particular. May I add that up to last June I had never attempted a political speech. Nothing was further from my mind than politics. I had attended only one political meeting since the war until my own convention was held. But there was a growing feeling among t'he farmers in my part of the country that they should be represented by a person who had been a farmer buff had not been tied down to any political party, whether Liberal, Conservative or Progressive. I regretted very much that the lot fell to me to represent them, for I felt that there were many farmers who were very much better qualified than I was to assume this great responsibility.

Agricultural Conditions
But they felt that I had one qualification that was necessary for the accomplishment of the task which they imposed upon me-I was a university graduate, little realizing, although I made it as clear to them as I could, that mathematics did not, any more than farming, give a person ability to speak. Therefore with this clear understanding and agreement that I have no political experience, I ask the indulgence of the house to-night. It is difficult enough to speak, it is still more difficult to think and translate one's thinking into parliamentary language.
I realize that my time is limited, very limited, to speak on a subject so comprehensive and important, and yet I feel that decent people throughout the Dominion,-and thank God the majority of the people of Canada are decent-would think that I was very remiss in my duty to-night if I let this opportunity pass to answer in as emphatic a manner as with my limited capacity I am capable of, the many cowardly attacks that have been made, more especially the most' cowardly of all this afternoon. From thd beginning of this session until now I think the attack this afternoon has been the most cowardly of all.
Some bon. MEMBERS: Order.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen
on the other side at the very outset pointed to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) as "the autocrat", "the great I am." Do they think they can fool intelligent people that way? Nothing could be clearer than the facts as they stand revealed. The right hon. Prime Minister has been returned election after election by the freest thinking people in the Dominion-the people of the cow town, city of Calgary, where they are accustomed to think straight, to talk straight, and, in days gone by to shoot straight. Do my friends opposite think that a city of free thinking people would idolize an autocrat? Does the right hon. the Prime Minister's return election after election show he has lost the common touch, that his heart does not vibrate in unison with the common people, that his mind does not think along the lines of the free-thinking men of the west? There' are no politics in Calgary.

they had lived here years before, and practically the only real qualification that seemed to be necessary for their appointment was that they were bosom friends of some of the chief Liberal organizers in the city. I say there are no politics in Calgary.
