maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
There are a few
transient Liberals, I repeat, a few civil servants; but the others are not Conservative; they do not vote Conservative, they vote for Bennett. There is another city in. the west, that dearly beloved city of Prince Albert. It is a city peculiarly situated and it has had a unique history. It is situated between the old settled district and the new or pioneering district. There is nowhere in Canada where the pioneering spirit has been kept so much alive as in the city of Prince Albert. What that pioneering spirit means only you who have lived in the west know. That spirit is this, that even though your house be a shack, or your bam merely a small place to shelter your cattle and your horses, it is a religion of the pioneers of the west that they will never turn anyone from their doors, whether black or white. Is it any wonder then when there appeared in Prince Albert a political outcast from eastern Canada, that nothing could be more natural than for those people to take him in? But let him beware. There is a difference between a night's lodging and thrusting yourself upon a hospitable and generous people as a permanent boarder. At the first election they accepted him out of generosity. But how was their hospitality responded to? At the meeting during the past election that was supposed to be a public meeting all the available policemen were on hand to keep order! That was the Liberal answer to the hospitality of the people of Prince Albert. But the city of Prince Albert gave its answer as a city on election day. The point I wish to make is this. I hate to say things that seem to hurt, but it has been so incessantly repeated in this house that the right hon. Prime Minister is an autocrat that I think it is only fair I should give the facts as the people of Canada see them. On the one hand we have the so-called "autocrat", who has been returned election after election with increasing majorities; on the other hand we have the right hon. gentleman whose heart bleeds for the common people, who weeps with them in then-sufferings, and whose sympathies are with them always. Yet he moves from one part of Canada to the other to get a seat.
It has been said that there is no man in Canada big enough to formulate a policy in

Agricultural Conditions

agriculture. No one realizes that better than I do. After I received my portfolio my first utterance was that no one realized better than I did my' many' limitations, and that I should seek every occasion for consultation with experts. I have been ready to receive constructive suggestions from persons in any walk of life. I have asked hoa. members to give me any constructive ideas that would be of benefit to the agriculture of Canada. I did not want people to think that in some subtle way' I was trying to steal their ideas. Therefore I made it 'clear that 1 would take every' opportunity to give credit where credit was due. As long as the idea was such as if put into practice w'ould redound to the advantage of agriculture in Canada, I was willing to give credit to the originator. That was the only reward I wished. I told you I had no political experience. It may be of interest to some hon. gentlemen to know that I did not even run my election as a Conservative, but as an independent Conservative. I made the statement at the convention that I wished to be free to vote as I saw fit in the interests of the farmers of Canada. I made that pledge on the 6th day of June and it was on that pledge that I took this trust from them. And I will keep that trust. I speak to-night, then, only as a farmer and in the simple language of the farm.
No one was more surprised than I was when the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) called me to ask me to take the portfolio of agriculture. I made it clear to him that I had no political experience and that I felt that was absolutely essential to make a success of such a gigantic undertaking. His answer was characteristic. He said, "I called you not to be a minister of politics but Minister of Agriculture." His attitude has been the same from that day to this, and I have no hesitation in saying that there was never a minister of agriculture in Canada who enjoyed in fuller measure the wholehearted support of the Prime Minister, his chieftain, and that of his colleagues than I have done. If there is any falling-down in the Department of Agriculture the responsibility is mine and mine alone.
And now for a few minutes with reference to agriculture, because I realize my time is brief. It was emphasized the other day-I do not know why' special attention should have been called to the fact, but I am glad it was,-'that I had resided only three years on a farm. It was said, with reference to certain gentlemen here, that all they knew about farming was looking through the fence on to the farm. I couple that statement with a suggestion which the hon. member for Melville
(Mr. R. Weir.]
(Mr. Motherwell), the former Minister of Agriculture, made-the only supposed constructive suggestion, I believe, which has come from the hon. gentleman since the house has been in session. It was this. He advised me in connection with cut worms to send people to a certain district to get caterpillars or larvae and to incubate those caterpillars to see whether the eggs laid by moths were fertile. I shall never forget the picture I saw opposite as I sat beside the Prime Minister. When the former Minister of Agriculture made that statement there was a nod of approval and of confidence on the part of the right hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), who was looking in my direction, as much as to say, "You see what twenty-two years' experience as Minister of Agriculture can do." Other farmers from the west on the other side also nodded their approval. That is what practice does. Well, certainly even the chief entomologist of our department will acknowledge that there is no man in his department with such deep, intensive scientific knowledge or insight as to be able to tell by incubating caterpillars whether the eggs laid by moths are fertile or not.
Maybe I have resided only three years on a farm, maybe there are other gentlemen on this side who know nothing about farming beyond what they have seen by looking through the fence. But could they know less by standing outside and looking through the fence, than if they were as completely asleep as old King Tut himself, to whom the hon. gentleman referred?
I must be fair. I said hon. gentleman opposite. I did not have time to watch the faces of all as closely as I might have done. But I did observe this. The thoughtful member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) showed by his smile that he appreciated the humour of the situation. The member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner), with his Scotch humour, also smiled and looked around to see whether some of the hon. members on the other side did not, with him, relish the humour that was taken so seriously. And the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) almost bubbled over before the statement was well out of the mouth of the former Minister of Agricrdture. But enough of that. No one, Mr. Speaker, is freer to admit his limitations than I am. I have missed no opportunity of asking for advice, and here let me say that some of the best advice I have received towards the formation of agricultural policy has come from hon. gentlemen opposite in the far corner of the chamber.

Agricultural Conditions
And now for agriculture. I hesitated as to what plan I should take to-night, whether to outline policies or to start at the beginning and follow them in chronological order as problems came before us. I have decided upon the latter. One of the first propositions I ran into was a method of obtaining a market for cattle that were in Canada, seeing that it was impossible for us to get a market in the United States by reason of the high tariff wall there. I made inquiries, even before the by-election, as to what ships were available and what boats might be fitted out. And here is the situation as I found it. Although I have referred to this on many occasions, I attach no blame to anyone. But the first obstacle came in the answer of the steamship companies, that on a previous occasion a former minister of the crown had advised them to fit their boats to carry cattle, promising so many head for so many shipments. The steamship companies went to the expense of fitting their boats, and the promise was not carried out. I do not blame anyone for not doing things that were impossible, but I do think that if some precaution had been observed, and this promise had not been given, it would be much easier now to persuade the steamship companies to carry out the refitting of their boats in order to transport Canadian cattle. However, realizing the situation, I immediately got in touch with professional experts

I do not mean so-called educated professional experts, but men who knew their business. I got in touch with five or six of the leading ranchers of the west; because I considered that the men with whom I could best discuss the cattle situation were men engaged in the cattle business. I wired them to meet me in Regina, and we consulted as to the best course to take. We decided to make two trial shipments, in which would be included cattle of different types. I got one of the best cattle men in the west to go along with the shipment so as to be able to put these cattle before the old country market in the most convincing way. In this shipment were groups of different types, and the man selected to put the cattle on the English market was Mr. Shea Gilchrist. He made the necessary arrangements and did everything within his power to create interest in the old land in this and any other shipments that might be made. I saw the cattle before they left Montreal, and I felt that the best advertisement which we could have in the old country for Canadian cattle was this representative shipment. I thought that we could have no better advertisement than to make 22110-S7.V
sure that some of the most suitable cattle would go into the hands of feeders. To encourage this, and to make certain that these cattle would not be slaughtered, it was agreed that we should subsidize them to pay freight up to five dollars a head. Although I made that proposal on Saturday-it was not a binding promise but merely a suggestion-the news immediately got to the old country. It appeared in the newspapers there that the Canadian government was subsidizing cattle and I had to withdraw the tentative promise made. However, I asked Mr. Gilchrist to take every precaution to see that this special shipment was not sold but put into the hands of some feeder, especially a leading farmer, in order that English farmers might see in the old country the type of cattle we had. He was very successful. He got them into the hands of one of the most outstanding north of England feeders. He went to see them twice before he left, and he assures me that nothing could be a better advertisement for our western cattle than this shipment. Later shipments went to Glasgow, and we arranged that some of these cattle should also go to feeders. The results were not as encouraging as we might have expected. But I went west in January to make arrangements for a shipment this spring and was surprised to find how pleased the ranchers were with the results of the four shipments we had made. Some of the cattle, the heavier type, brought three dollars a head more than they would have done in the local market, and although some of the lighter cattle were sold for less than they would have brought locally, it was the unanimous opinion of the ranchers there that the price of cattle in the west had been held up from half to three-quarters of a cent per pound. That is not my opinion; it is the opinion of men in the business.
A simple mathematical calculation will show what that half cent a pound wdth that volume meant to the cattlemen of western Canada. When I made my trip to Calgary in January I was following a policy which I hope always to follow while 1 continue in the position I now occupy, and that is, that no politics will in any way be allowed to interfere with agriculture. The only man whom I notified when I made my second visit to Calgary was Senator Riley, and I do not think any person can accuse him of being a rabid Conservative. He met me in the hotel and introduced me to the cattlemen. We stayed there and made plans for the handling of cattle this spring, but I do not think that is sufficient; we need plans to extend into the future so that we shall not continue in any
Agricultural Conditions

haphazard way to formulate plans, only when faced with an emergency. We endeavoured to obtain all the information we could as to cattle on feed in the west, the types of cattle, where they were situated, and so on; and in addition we made arrangements with the transportation systems to give us a 50 per cent freight rate from the ranges to the coarse grain feed lands in northern Saskatchewan. That would save an extra toll-that is the only word I can use, because it seems to me that from the time produce leaves the farm until it gets into the mouths of the consumers it is one toil after another. As practical farmers we endeavoured to find ways of saving a dollar here or a dollar there, whether by freight, commission or otherwise, because it is often those few dollars which mean the differeuce between profit and loss. We made arrangements not only for the shipment of these cattle to the northern feed lands at 50 per cent of the regular freight rate, but also for reductions in the expense of the farmer going down to hunt those cattle. We arranged that he would be able to obtain accurate information and it is hoped by next fall or possibly late summer that the farmers in the north will be able to obtain cattle according to their requirements at a minimum expense.
In addition to that we felt that many farmers in Saskatchewan had had very little experience in feeding cattle and that it was only fair that this machinery should be put into their hands for immediate use. Simple experiments were carried on with the homegrown feeds. I asked the experimental farm at Rosthern to perform experiments on some eighteen or twenty head of steers and heifers, sired by the one bull so that the strain would be uniform and there would be the least variation possible in the results. I asked them to feed cut sheaves and crushed barley to one group, and cut sheaves and crushed wheat to another group, in both cases with salt and water only. Many people thought that we would not have any success with feed such as that, but realized that many farmers in western Canada have had no experience in feeding and they would want things to be as simple as possible. After allowing for the freight on the cattle and the purchase price, they were sold eighty-four days afterward on a basis which returned $1.19 per bushel for wheat and 83 cents per bushel for barley.
One of the most difficult problems we had to face was the impossibility of shipping these cattle to the United States. Regulations and restrictions had been put on the shipment of cattle by the British government-we knew* of this last November but no announcement
Mr. R. Weir.]
was made. Announcement was made some two months later that there was an embargo against Canadian cattle. It was announced also that there were 100,000 cattle in western Canada for export, and the result of such an announcement was evident; the people thought that they would be unable to get rid of their cattle; they threw them on the market and the price went down. We were able to counteract this to some extent. It will be of interest to the cattlemen in the house that we have every available foot of space to be secured in British ships this summer to carry our cattle to the old land.
The next problem had to do with butter. It has been said that the raising of the duty on butter encouraged a lot of people to go into the dairy industry with the result that the prices on butter were broken. That is not my interpretation of the cause. I believe that the price of wheat and the price of coarse grain was such as to encourage people to enter this industry; they were ready to go into anything which would make them five or ten cents with which to carry them through the winter. In order to save this industry we put, on an eight-cent duty against New Zealand butter. However, the Australian treaty, made by the previous government, was still in force and that permitted a one-cent duty only against Australian butter. We were faced with a flood of Australian butter, and my colleagues and I realized that the only way to meet this emergency was to make a verbal agreement with the Hon. Parker Moloney of Australia to the effect that Australia would not release in Canada any butter under 32 cents per pound except with our consent. This at least helped the daily industry of this country through the winter months. There was a possibility at one time that the price would be driven down by New Zealand because they were shipping in some butter to sell at less than 32 cents. I immediately got in touch with the commissioner for New Zealand and was able to arrange with him that their butter would not be released at a price less than 32 cents per pound to the detriment of our dairying industry. This state of affairs lasted until some two weeks ago, when the increased production of butter in Canada drove the price still lower. In my opinion, one of the reasons for this drop is the lack of a uniform board of control in Canada to supervise this industry. For the benefit of those who have expressed adverse opinions, I will say that when we came into power Canadian butter was selling at a lower price than that prevailing in the United States, and Australian butter

Agricultural Conditions
in England, and I believe New Zealand butter as well. Immediately after coming into power we put on a duty of eight cents per pound; from then and for some six or eight months our butter was selling at a higher price than was butter in London and the United States. That continued, as I said before, until some ten days or two weeks ago.
The butter industry is almost to the export level; we expect it to be at that level within a short time. I am told by the dairy commissioner and by produce merchants that our Canadian butter as a whole is not sufficiently uniform as to grade to permit its being labelled and shipped to the old country as Canadian butter. The former Minister of Agriculture, recommended the other day that some of the creameries in Quebec should be merged into larger creameries in an endeavour to develop a more uniform grade of butter. Surely this is not the time to do that. While listening to the hon. gentleman's remarks, I could not help but think that if he had done one-tenth as much during the nine years he was in office as he said he had hoped to do or intended to do if he were returned to office, we would not be having insistent demands from hon. gentlemen on the other side for a statement of agricultural policy.
When this government came into power, realizing the then low price of coarse grains and rough feed, we felt that we would soon be in the export market with our bacon. Upon making investigation, one point was evident to hon. gentlemen on both sides of the house -or at least it was evident to the government,-namely the great scarcity of select bacon, the only type that has any opportunity to compete in the old country with the Danish product. In Saskatchewan alone I found that the number of select bacon hogs was only 5-6 per cent; that is, only 5-6 per cent of the pigs slaughtered in Saskatchewan would have any opportunity to go on the world market. That is the condition in which I found the bacon industry for purposes of export. I knew there had to be an emergency measure, and it was an emergency measure when I tried to work out a way that would make it easier for the farmers to get into the production of a select bacon type of pigs. That is why I formulated the "brood sow" policy that some hon. gentlemen opposite have been making a good deal of fun of. In that way we made it easier for the farmers to get into the production of the select bacon type of pigs. Further, this idea was that litters of the. select bacon type of brood sows would be sired by boars of the select bacon type, and the information brought to me is that one could not realize how much effect this would be likely to have on the type
of pigs obtained from these litters for breeding purposes.
The next point with which I wish to deal is breeding cattle. I think, as perhaps one of the soundest principles of agriculture, whether in live stock or feeding, we should at all times aim to get into our live stock that type of blood that will make the best use of the feed that we give them, whether dairy cattle or beef cattle. It was for that reason I tried to catch up with the policies that had been neglected so much, by introducing the policy that was scoffed at this afternoon, the policy known as the "bull loaning" policy, by which we hope to help the farmers of Canada, especially at this time by loaning them bulls under supervision. This was only doing fairly and honestly as the people of Canada would really wish, because I believe ninety-nine per cent of our people are really intensely interested in this question of the success of agriculture and desire from the bottom of their hearts that agriculture should prosper.
In connection with statements of hon. gentlemen opposite concerning agriculture, people both on this side and on the other have told me not to take these debates too seriously; that hon. gentlemen on the other side who moved and supported this motion were not so much concerned with policies of agriculture; that it was all a political game. I can scarcely believe that. I have sat here day after day watching the faces of hon. gentlemen opposite, farmers from the west, and I cannot help feeling they are very sincere as regards their interest in helping agriculture. I am willing at this point to put it to hon. members; I will ask the hon. gentleman who moved the amendment if he cannot show to the house that he is interested in agriculture and describe the two brood sow policies of the late government when they went out of office. I realize that he will hesitate to interrupt me in my speech. No doubt the hon. gentleman knows those policies, but if he does not, then I would be left to believe that the suggestion that the talk was political rather than agricultural is true. We have other so-called policies and I realize that each of them is not of very great importance in itself for immediate relief. The hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donne'lly) said this afternoon that these things were all right in their way, and I appreciate the kindly reference to them. However, I ask, would they not have been much more right if they had been put into force five years ago, so that now we would be in the position in which we should be?
It has been said that this government has done nothing for agriculture. Laughing reference has been made to the speeches that I
Agricultural Conditions

delivered in Toronto and Montreal in connection with the banks not lending money, and especially to the last part of my speech. I did not make those speeches in western Canada to the farmers. I thought the place to make them, the place where the farmers of western Canada would wish me to make them, would be in Toronto and Montreal, and that is where I made them. At the end of my speech in Montreal I said that if credit were not given to the farmers through the banks, some steps would have to be taken to give them credit. The reference has been made that we have heard no more of that. The truth is that in less than ten days from that time, realizing that credit would not be given, I made arrangements to meet the western ministers of agriculture at Winnipeg just for the purpose of doing what I said would have to be done. I met with them and we discussed the problems of the west, seed grain relief, relief to help the farmers to put in grain, and other relief. These ministers agreed it would be better in the interests of carrying out this plan if our part in the contract were not made public, but I can say this, that never before was there a government which realized more clearly than we did the exigencies of the situation of the western farmer due to circumstances over which he had no control, and our offer was commensurate with our appreciation of the situation. Moreover, when it is known, I am sure hon. gentlemen opposite will blush for having discussed this question in the way they have done, although perhaps this is through no fault of their own as they did not know the offer.
In conclusion, because I see I have only five minutes more, no one in the house realizes better than I do that these policies which I have enunciated, are policies that will not result in benefits until some time in the future. No one realizes better than I do that there is carried by the western farmer a load that requires some form of immediate relief, a load that these policies will not immediately alleviate. But that load of mortgages and debts was not created since last August. That is the load that worries me, when I look forward to the future to see these agricultural communities in the west happy and prosperous again, as I would see them.
There is another handicap for which we take no responsibility. In the early days when western Canada was first settled, people came from many countries, including many from the United States, with whole carloads af equipment and were directed to areas that people knew or should have known did not

give those farmers a ghost of a chance of making a living there. Why was that done? They were warned about it. Among many others, that veteran rancher Joe Wylie, from Maple Creek, told them they were breaking up over night a sod that took a thousand years to make. That is one of the loads we are carrying in western Canada to-day.
Another load is that of weeds. In this connection I hesitate to make this statement, but I think when we are discussing in this house things on their merits, we are not supposed to mince words and therefore I shall speak plainly. However, before I discuss weeds, it has been advocated that a pork packing plant be established in the west. Few hon. members in the house or in the Dominion have given more thought to that question than I have since last October. I have been in consultation with people who, I thought, might operate it. I have done something to bring representatives of wholesale cooperative houses from the old country to look into the proposition, because I felt nothing like that could be a success unless we had some one here from the old land who knew the taste of the English people in regard to bacon, to manage the plant, etc. We could use their sales machinery. I believed that in this way thousands of dollars would be saved. I have made a study of private plants, of public plants; the whole thing has been gone into very thoroughly. I doubt whether the quantity of bacon this year will be anything like what people some time ago expected it would be, but if hon. gentlemen opposite were anxious for a packing plant, they had plenty of opportunity to build one. Take the Moose Jaw registered seed grain plant at Moose Jaw. There was enough money spent on that to build four seed cleaning plants and then have enough left over to build a packing plant. According to the speech delivered by the provincial treasurer in Saskatchewan the other day, the co-operative creameries that were built there lost the province one million dollars. That was enough to build at least four packing plants in Saskatchewan. If the estimate for the railway hotel in Saskatoon had been cut in two, enough would have been saved to build a packing plant in every province in the Dominion.
One word more and I shall have finished. I think the biggest load that agriculture in Canada, especially in Saskatchewan has to carry, is known to the majority of farmers in this Dominion. When the former Minister of Agriculture was made Minister of Agriculture in the government of Saskatchewan in 1905, he had before him a clean, fertile, virgin field

Agricultural Conditions
in that province, and he had coming into that field people who took second place to none. And what has been the result? It is an old saying that there is a record written that he who runs may read; but written along trails leading out of Regina there is a record which those who drive in automobiles travelling sixty miles an hour can read, a record written during the term of office of the former Minister of Agriculture in sow thistle, stinkweed and other weeds of various kinds.
But that is not all. He left the provincial ' field in 1918 and came into federal politics as Minister of Agriculture in 1921. His work was not yet completed. There was a patch in Saskatchewan that was still not weedy enough, that fertile valley which takes second place to none, that valley which is in the constituency I have the great honour to represent, the Carrot river valley in northern Saskatchewan. It *was comparatively clear and clean of weeds of any kind. What happened? The former Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart)-I take it that he acted in conjunction with the former Minister of Agriculture- decided that there was a great slough there which should be drained, and they drained it at a cost in the neighbourhood of $186,000- which would have helped considerably in building a packing plant.

I was just commencing to read from the remarks of the Prime Minister following those of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). The remarks of the Prime Minister continue as follows:
Mr. Bennett:	I tried to indicate the other
day that I think it is very much better that these things should speak for themselves. We put the collective credit of this country behind the, wheat market.
Mr. Vallance:	It was security only to the
banks which you gave, not to the wheat pool at all, or to the farmer. The help was given to the banks.

Agricultural Conditions
An hon. Member:	It was the banks you
saved.
Mr. Bennett:	I appeal to you, Mr. Speaker,
and through you to the Canadian people, to judge whether anything could better illustrate the line of thought indulged in by some hon. members than the two observations to which we have just listened.
One of those remarks was made by me and another by an hon. member whose name does not appear in Hansard. Then the Prime Minister continues:
Mr. Bennett: Could anything be better calculated to bring-shall I say?-despair on the part of those farmers who are struggling with adversity than this counsel of desperation to which we have been listening?
The Prime Minister used the words "struggling with adversity". Hon. members heard what the Minister of Agriculture said to-night.
The banks have money belonging to their depositors, and they owe it to them. The banks have no right to lend that money upon security which will hazard the deposit. The banks have lent the money to the farmers, to the pool -which was a voluntary organization created by the farmers themselves and not by the country. The banks were called upon to do one of two things; support that market by continuing to advance money; or stop doing so and let wheat drop 40 cents.
Then a question is asked by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young):
Would wheat have dropped 40 cents if you had not taken the action you did?
The reply of the Prime Minister is as follows:
I cannot say. I can only say that that is the judgment of those well able to express an opinion on the subject.
Mr. Young: That is 40 cents more than it actually did drop.
The Prime Minister was trying to convey the idea that through the assistance extended by this government to the wheat pool in the marketing of the crop the government had saved the price of wheat from dropping as low as 40 cents. I would ask the Prime Minister if the action taken by the government to prevent the price of wheat from dropping, also prevented a similar drop in the Argentine, Russia, the United States and Australia? I ask that question because at no time was the wheat of those countries any lower in price than that of Canada. It would appear that by his action he saved not only the Canadian market but the entire wheat market of the world. If we are to accept his statement we must come to that conclusion.
Now that the Prime Minister has stated his action in connection with the control of wheat prices I am going to ask him and the Minister of Agriculture to use every effort
possible to give to the western wheat growers 100 per cent control of their wheat. If the Prime Minister argues that by advancing or guaranteeing moneys to the banks he controlled the price of wheat I am now asking him to consider in a similar way the present demands of the western farmer. In the province of Saskatchewan we were attempting to have 100 per cent control by legislation. I noticed the other day in the press an article stating that in the courts our action had been declared ultra vires. I do not know what the next step will be; I do not know whether there will be an appeal to this government for an enactment which will enable them to have such legislation, or whether they will ask this government once more to create the old wheat board. After listening to and reading the statements of the Prime Minister I cannot see for the life of me why or how the government can refuse to take such action.
At one time we in western Canada had a cooperative organization known as the pool. I was rather grieved this afternoon to read the following from the Globe of May 7:
The pool permits members to suspend contracts and use open markets.
What does that mean? It means that we are -back to where we were five or six years ago. Only one thing can save us, and this government and this parliament have the power to put i-t through. I plead with them to take that action. I go further and say that this government is partly responsible for the defeat of the pool, and I shall proceed to prove it. Because of the position the pool got into and because of the assistance which was tendered by the banks the pool was being dictated to as to its policy by some powers other than those who were the contract signers. When the Prime Minister went to the Imperial conference he took with him some chief advisers. Who were they? He took two professors of economics, one from the university of Saskatchewan, Doctor Swanson, and Doctor MacGibbon, who is a professor of economics and also fills one of the chairs of the Board of Grain Commissioners. He took John I. McFarland. Then there was Mr. Gage, who is now deceased, and Alex. McPhail, who was president of the Saskatchewan wheat pool. As I said, we found that we owed the -banks. Probably it was our fault because we believed that -in the interests of the producer we should deviate from the old organized grain trade method of marketing whereby for every purchase made to-day they hedged to-morrow to secure the bank for the money advanced on the purchases made to-day. We cooperatives believing that that was not in the interests o'
Agricultural Conditions

the producer, decided that we were not going to sell futures wheat, hedge our wheat, and that we would give the banks security of 15 cents a bushel. When that margin almost disappeared the government did step in. It looks rather peculiar to me that not long after the Prime Minister and his associates had gone to the Imperial conference, I think about two weeks, we find Mr. McFarland returning to Canada, and shortly afterwards he becomes manager of the central selling agency of the Canadian pools. He took that position on two conditions; first, that he was to receive no salary-being a Scotchman, I suppose he did not want any money; second, that he foe given an absolutely free hand regarding the sales policy of the pools. It was quite evident to us who had taken an active part in building up the organization that this was the first body blow to the pools. I would not have been so suspicious had it not happened that the -day after the announcement was made that Mr. McFarland had accepted the managership of the selling agency, my genial friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) came out with the statement that he was pleased to see that the pools of their own free will had decided to give Mr. McFarland a free hand. I question the so-called "free will" because I know the pools. The first thing Mr. McFarland did was to close the overseas agency. What was the result? Let me read a despatch from France, the country that the Prime Minister has been telling us is going to buy large quantities of our wheat. This despatch is dated Paris, March IS, and is written by William H. Ingram, correspondent of the Times-Journal:
Since the Canadian wheat pool closed it3 offices in Paris, Canadian wheat is sold only through the grain trade. Millers know perfectly well that the traders are not doing business without a profit. They also know that in many cases the wheat which is offered to them has passed through middlemen who have increased the price a few cents, and this does not tend to please the buyer any more than it has added to the profit of the Canadian farmer.
The French people find it difficult to understand why the Paris office of the Canadian pool has been closed when millers willing to buy Canadian wheat without middlemen W'ere buying it under conditions which suited them. Prices were the same for every kind of buyer 

miller, merchant or broker. It was good business without a preferential tariff, buyers knowing that the prices were those quoted daily by Winnipeg.
During the seven years in which the Paris office functioned, there was not a single complaint against quality. Every miller ordering wheat from it was absolutely sure that he received the quality ordered. This was due to the fact that a bill of lading and a dominion

certificate were issued with every order from the smallest to the largest. And" this was an encouragement to the buyer.
Under existing conditions it may happen that only one bill of lading and one dominion certificate may be issued for, say, 1,000 tons which will be divided into ten lots of 100 tons each, but for which each miller will be unable to get the dominion certificate as proof that it is Canadian wheat which he is receiving. Any omission of that dominion certificate may result in the millers not getting Canadian wheat at all. And that is quite likely what is going to happen.
If information is correct, the same applied to Portugal and Spain.
Portugal has authorized recently the importation of foreign wheat for its own consumption. Representatives from the Soviet, the Danubian countries and the Argentine have been on the spot to bid closely for the quantity allowed. This has resulted in an order for 46,000 tons being given to the Argentine. If Canada had had her representatives there at the time, the chances are that she would have obtained the order or at least a part of it.
As to Italy, it is known that through reciprocal arrangement she is buying this year Soviet wheat in exchange for manufactured goods. It is unfortunate that Canada if losing by this arrangement one of her most important European customers. But as Soviet delivery is far from being satisfactory, it is expected that she may resume her former business relations with the dominion.
In the face of this, and the position that the cooperative organizations find themselves in to-day, and the statement of the Prime Minister the other day when he took credit that because of the fact he had guaranteed the banks against certain losses he was able to stabilize the price of wheat, I demand for the farmers of western Canada that he immediately, by enabling legislation, make if. possible to put over 100 per cent control as the farmers first sought, or establish the old Canada wheat board. I think the Minister of Agriculture will agree that that at least is a constructive suggestion to the government. I was rather disappointed that he did not say something about it.
I notice that the Minister of Agriculture referred also to a speech that he himself made in Toronto. The Prime Minister said in this house on April 28th:
Who is it that says the farmers are unfit for credit and that the country is bankrupt and insolvent? Day after day and week after week hon. gentlemen opposite-
Meaning us.
[DOT]-have been saying it; they complain that the farmers cannot get credit.
Now let me quote something that was said, not by any member of the opposition but by the Minister of Agriculture himself. This was long before the session opened; this was on February 4 at Toronto, and I think

Agricultural Conditions
13G7
the hon. minister must bear some of the responsibility of bringing to the attention of the country the fact that the farmers of the west to-day cannot get credit. If the Prime Minister was right in saying that those conditions did not exist, surely his Minister of Agriculture would not have said what I now present to the house. Let me read this Canadian Press despatch:
"Persons with glib tongues, with hopes of personal publicity," have been responsible for agitation among western farmers, Hon. Robert Weir. Canadian Minister of Agriculture, told a gathering of Canadian agriculturists at a Canadian National exhibition annual dinner to live stock breeders.
These persons, the minister said, had gone around to the farmers exhorting them to prevail upon the government to have wheat "pegged" at $1 a bushel, demand new freight rates and eliminate mortgage interests. Mr. Weir made it clear he in no way referred to the United Farmers.
I think if the Minister of Agriculture had gene to the trouble to read the memorandum that the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section, presented to the Prime Minister on December 30 last, he would not have had occasion to say that he was not referring to the United Farmers, because everything that was asked for by the "agitators", as he called them, was embodied in that memorandum. He continues:
In spite of this agitation, he declared he found at a recent meeting of his own constituency no trace of dissatisfaction and no complaints. He had warned them they might have to accept extremely low prices for their products, and still there had been no complaints. he said.
Now, this was the point:
Conditions, he admitted, were severe in some cases, particularly concerning credit. It was credit the farmer needed and he was unable to get_ it. While not criticizing the banks. Mr. Weir said he was unable to understand why these institutions refused to allow money to these people. He would not advocate the loan of money to people without justifiable security, but people who had ample assets in their farms and properties were not able to secure relief in this form and they needed money to carry on.
The Prime Minister conveyed the impression to the house and to the country that the whole controversy regarding the economic position of the western farmer was started by the opposition at the opening of the session. I have just read a Canadian press despatch of a statement made by the Minister of Agriculture on February 4. Probably had he not made that statement many of us would not have really realized just how bad a condition the western farmer was in; but when even the Minister of Agriculture-who was back here in Ottawa, not living through the conditions
that we in the west were familiar with every day-had noticed those conditions, surely the Prime Minister will not condemn us for having brought them to the attention of the country and to his attention. We are still looking for relief. It will be remembered how the Prime Minister when out in the west during the elections, used to say to the farmers:
Listen, you agriculturists from the west and all the other parts of Canada, you have been taught to mock at tariffs and applaud free trade. Tell me, when did free trade fight for you? Tell me, when did free trade fight for you? You say tariffs are only for the manufacturers. I will make them fight for you as well. I will use them to blast a way into the markets that have been closed to you.
I ask you, Mr. Speaker, I ask this house, has he demonstrated to the smallest extent that he has obtained for the farmer any greater market than he had before? The one thing the farmer needs above all others is a market; and as was pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly), the action of this government has made it more difficult to obtain that market. In making it more difficult for goods to come into Canada, the Prime Minister has made it that much more difficult for the agriculturist of Canada to sell his surplus produce; because, whether hon. gentlemen opposite believe it or not, we must take payment for our exports by imports. That is the only thing we can do, and every time you restrict the possibility of our shipping out one bushel of wheat by raising the tariff on any commodity which we import, you make it all the more difficult for the farmer of the west to operate. I think the Minister of Agriculture will admit this as a westerner. He will admit it as a westerner and not as a politician or as Minister of Agriculture. As a plain farmer he will agree that that statement is absolutely true.

speechtext: May I ask a question?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
I will allow the hon.
member to ask a question.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend. I ask this as a fair question. How is it that, in spite of the statement which the hon. member makes, the exports of wheat during the last eight months have been from sixty to seventy million bushels more than they were in the corresponding eight months of the previous year?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
I will tell my hon. friend the reason. The farmer is selling it; or rather, as the hon. member for Willow Bunch pointed out, he is not selling it but giving it away. After twenty-five years of farming in the west
Agricultural Conditions

and marketing many thou,sands of bushels of wheat; after harvesting last year one of the best crops ever grown in that section of western Canada, the section in which I live; after seeing oats last year running as high as 80, 90 and 100 bushels to the acre, and wheat going from 20 to 45 bushels per acre, and finding the farmers insolvent to-day-after all this experience, I would not dare to tell you, Mr. Speaker, of some of the conditions that prevail among large farmers. And the larger the farmer the harder he was hit. With this statement, again, I think the Minister of Agriculture will agree; because you cannot produce wheat any more economically-perhaps slightly more-by increased production than if you produced only a 20 bushel crop. I say this for the reason that your initial cost is the same-your seed and cultivation, and your operations right up to the moment you start harvesting the crop, although from that point on you decrease your cost because of volume. But so long as you cannot get cost of production, I care not whether it be a cent or ten cents below cost, the more you produce the more you lose. That is the position of the western farmer to-day.
I would urge most seriously upon the government the absolute necessity of taking some definite action. This is not a time for palaver. As I listened to the Minister of Agriculture- I hate to refer to this again but I must-I really did expect that he would deal with these most urgent problems, the most important of which is finding a profitable market for Canadian wheat. The Prime Minister stated that he had, by his efforts, saved wheat from going to 40 cents, and if he is able to save it from going to 40 cents, then I should think that a man of his calibre ought to be able to raise it another 20 cents, even if he has to resort to pegging, as suggested by the organized farmers themselves.
I do not wish to cover old territory, Mr. Speaker. I could point out, as others have done, that we have pegged the price of everything else. But I would repeat that every time you raise the duty on any article coming into Canada you make it so much more difficult for the farmer to find a place for his wheat in the world's market. I do not believe the tariff ,is sound economically, and the greatest economists to-day are telling us that our most difficult problem lies in the high tariff walls that are dividing the people of the earth. If, therefore, we could remove those walls and have a free exchange of commodities as between country and country, I am sure that the problems with which we are faced at the present time would be largely solved.

It is all very well for the Minister of Agriculture to institute bull, sow and other policies. But they are as old as the hills. The best live stock ever raised on God's earth never resulted from such policies as the minister is advocating. I know, Mr. Speaker, coming from the country across the sea in which I was born, that Canada is not adapted in some sections to some of the enterprises which the minister would force upon the country. Look at the country in which I was brought up, Scotland: they have never had any bull and sow policies or anything of that kind. The country is naturally adapted to the production of live stock. And as the hon. member for Willow Bunch pointed out this afternoon, it is ridiculous to expect the farmers of the west to go into mixed farming. The farmer of western Canada does not wish to go further into debt; what he wants is an opportunity to get out of his present financial difficulties. This five million dollars is just so much piffle; I would not even consider it.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
I see the hon. member
for Saskatoon laughing. I listened with others the other night to what he said, and I read his remarks, and I can assure him that when the people have an opportunity to register their views regarding the actions of this government in this matter they will do so in no uncertain manner.
I would impress upon the Minister of Agriculture that the supreme problem facing agriculture to-day is the finding of a market for our wheat. The hon. gentleman admits, Mr. Speaker, that his is the voice that speaks for agriculture within the cabinet councils of the nation, and there is therefore a great responsibility upon him. And I believe he feels that responsibility. All you need to do is merely to look at the hon. gentleman and you will realize that he is conscious of his responsibility in this matter, and I hope that he is man enough, big enough to rise to the occasion against all the plutocrats sitting around him in the cabinet and stand up for the rights of the farmers of Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
I know the house is just about ready for the question, but seeing that it is the will of parliament that hon. members should vote upon every issue, I do not propose to vote until I have published my reasons for doing so.
I am sorry I cannot enter into the debate with that warmth which was characteristic of the speech made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir), or with the heat which evidently was engendered thereby in the

Agricultural Conditions
breast of the hon. member who has jusit taken his seat (Mr. Vallanee). I do not see much difference between the debate which is now going on and the one at the conclusion of which we voted a short time ago. Nor do I see much difference between this debate and many others which it has been my pleasure to follow in this House of Commons.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: What is the use of talking then?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
I will tell the hon. gentleman in a few moments what the use of talking is, because I am not going to talk for the sake of a party or in any hope that some day this little group will be on the right of Mr. Speaker. I am going to speak on the issue as I see it, without any frills on either side of it.
Before addressing myself specifically to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown), I wish to make a reference to the speech of the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh). This afternoon the hon. gentleman went a long piece out of his way to make an attack on me because of a speech I made in this house some time ago. He did not attack the speech itself but merely an aside in that speech, w'hich made a reference to secession talk in the west. As some other hon. members have done, he attributed to me the blame for, or the honour, as the case may be, of first introducing that question in the House of Commons this session. I just wish to call the attention of the house and of the Ottawa Journal to the fact that I was not the first to mention that question in the house; the first one to mention it in the house was the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull). He quoted the ex-premier of [DOT]Saskatchewan in his reference to the matter. The next hon. member to mention it was the member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallanee), who even went so far as to hold aloft that famous "Charter of Liberty" drawn up in the province of Saskatchewan. The next hon. member to refer to the matter was the deputy speaker of the house (Mr. LaVergne). These hon. gentlemen scoffed at the idea but in my reference to it I said only that I thought perhaps the hon. gentlemen did not understand as well as they might the conditions prevailing in the west and that there might be more in the secession talk than was imagined. That remark acted as a match to the powder barrel of the Ottawa Journal and hurt the feelings of my hon. friend to my right who made a reference to it this afternoon. I trust that this will be sufficient to prove to my hon. friend that I was not the first to mention the matter in this house.
I shall now address myself to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). In doing so I would say in all kindness that the Liberal party is always great in opposition but I am afraid that if they are not careful they will prove themselves to be so great that the country will want to keep them always in that position. The hon. member for Lisgar is one of the most respected members in this house. He is possessed of a matured and balanced judgment, is well informed on all matters pertaining to agriculture and has advanced in this chamber on many occasions very interesting views on agricultural economics. I listened to his speech on his amendment, I have since read it very carefully and I must confess that I agree with a great deal of what he said. I do not think he overstated the case in referring to the conditions prevailing in the west and I stand with him in his earnestness and sincerity to endeavour to find some means of alleviation and in looking forward to some policy to safeguard a return of normal conditions. Nevertheless, when I come to examine his amendment I do not feel so much in keeping with his thoughts. I intend to oppose that amendment, and will give my reasons for so doing.
The amendment does not make a definite, constructive proposal. It was moved as a protest against the speech of the Prime Minister. What I am about to say may not be popular in the west, or in my own riding, because of the fact that the Prime Minister's speech referred to did meet with some resentment. I agree with my hon. friend that that speech will be regarded by the western farmer as indicative of a lack of sympathy, but I believe that when the western farmer understands the relief actually given by this government he will then realize that when the Prime Minister made that speech he knew that conditions in the west were bad indeed.
The suggestion as to markets made in the last paragraph of the amendment is too vague and nebulous to warrant one's voting nonconfidence in a government which has not been in office one year, furthermore, the amendment is unfair to the Minister of Agriculture who has just taken over the responsibilities of office.
The amendment regrets that the administration has failed to implement its promises with respect to agriculture and that it has not announced any policy. I thought that the last election was singularly empty of promises so far as agriculture was concerned. That was one of the objections we had in my riding to the Conservative party; that it
Agricultural Conditions

made no promises to agriculture but had made a great many to the other classes. It may be that in the province from which my hon. friend come such promises were made, but so far as the keeping of promises is concerned, we feel that we can deal with the government on that score at the proper time. I do not think it is fair inside of one year to expect the government to have made a very definite impression upon the economic conditions prevailing in Canada.
Speaking of agriculture specifically, I think the hon. Minister of Agriculture put his finger on the point when he referred to the fact that the conditions from which agriculture is suffering were not developed during the last nine months but had been developing during the last nine years. I do not blame the previous government for having developed these conditions because there are many reasons apart from anything the past government could have done to account for the present state of western agriculture, and in all fairness we must admit that present day conditions have not been brought, about by the advent of the present administration. As to a policy not having been announced, I think the Prime Minister stated in one of his speeches that the Minister of Agriculture would announce his policy when he brought down his estimates. I am quite prepared to give the Minister of Agriculture and the government at least one year in which to deal with agriculture and other matters of importance in Canada. I do not know what they intend to do; I do not know that we will be any better off next year than we are this year, but I owe it to my own sense of fairness to give the government that opportunity. If my hon. friend is still of the same opinion next year-he probably will be even though the government may have done something by that time-I will then stand with him in criticism of the government if it has failed to take advantage of its opportunity to do something.
The amendment next refers to the policies ol the administration restricting rather than expanding trade. I am at a loss to understand just what the hon. gentleman means by this, because in the first clause he denounces the government for not having a policy and in the next clause complains that the policy of the government is a restriction of trade. It may be that he had the belief that the general policy of the government restricted trade and no policy has been announced for agriculture. If that were the hon. gentleman's belief then the clauses would

have some meaning, but if he referred in both cases to a general policy, then there would be a direct contradiction.
The amendment then goes on to state that without the development of international trade Canadian agriculture will become increasingly paralyzed. In this regard I refer to the statement made by the previous speaker (Mr. Vallance) in answer to a question asked by the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion). The hon. minister asked the question: How is it that more wheat is being sold this year than last, to which the hon. member for South Battleford replied that it was being given away this year. I agree with him in his answer, but it was given away last year as well and in that respect he was unfair. Wheat is being sold this year at the world price just as it was sold last year on that basis, therefore both this government and the last government are in exactly the same position in relation to the price of wheat.
The amendment states that any policy brought forward with respect to agriculture should include emergency measures to meet the present crisis. According to the statement just made by the Minister of Agriculture, an emergency policy has been in force for some time. I understand that he went to Winnipeg in January last; that he met there representatives of the western provinces; that an agreement or arrangement was made which was satisfactory to the premiers of the western provinces in respect to certain relief, and that for some good reason on the part of the western provinces, the actual conditions of the agreement, so far as they had to do with the federal government, were not made public; so that would appear to settle the emergency part of the resolution with which we are dealing.
Finally, the suggestion is that adequate provision should be made for the processing of meats and the marketing of live stock, wheat, dairy, and all other agriculture products. That, of course, should be done, but I have not heard any hon. member, nor have I heard any one outside of the house, put forward a single proposal that would be calculated to bring a cent more for wheat than we are now getting. If the hon. member who moved this amendment will put forward a concrete proposal that will give even a promise of a penny more a bushel, I shall vote for it, but so far in all the speeches that have been delivered in the house this session, I have not heard a proposal that would raise the price of wheat or pork or eggs or butter or any other commodity. Indeed, this par-

Agricultural Conditions
liament would have great difficulty in altering materially the price of any one of these commodities. I think hon. gentlemen who expect, that or talk as if they expected it, know better. They know that our present system and the conditions under which we are living and operating are such that laws not passed by parliament, but laws of economic significance, determine the price of all these commodities, and that no proposal which could be made by parliament, so far as I am aware, apart from actually bonusing wheat or pegging the price, would produce the result that we desire. The government has stated very emphatically that it will not peg the price of wheat, and I am not sure that I want it to do so. I question very much the economic sense of such a proposition and I have done so ever since it was first made. I have expressed my opinion in that regard in other places than in this chamber.
But with regard to relief for farmers, the government can take action, and as regards the debt which is on the back of the farmers, which did not come last year, but which has been accumulating and accumulating for a generation due to a bad policy of finance which has been adopted by all governments and due to unrestricted interest rates and other things from which agriculture has been suffering, that burden of debt might be relieved by some arrangement which the government might make. It might be possible to fix the interest at a lower rate or to get the mortgage companies to think reasonable in regard to the situation and to cancel the interest for last year and the year before so as to give the farmers an opportunity to come back when conditions improve. The government maybe could not do that by law, but they might be able to do it by consultation and advice. Apart from that I do not believe any suggestion has been made that would guarantee to the farmers even a hope of getting a higher price for wheat.
While that is so, we have here a motion of no confidence moved against a government that is really sitting now in its first session, because it has not raised the price of wheat or found a better market for wheat or other things. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I am very anxious to find a better market for the western farmers; I am very anxious to see them get more for their wheat, and I say again if any hon. gentleman on this or the other side of the house will put forward an idea that will give a hope of doing that, I shall readily vote for it, no matter what party he belongs to. But in the first session of a government that has not
been in power one year, to move a vote of no confidence in them for not getting a better market and to do this without making a suggestion of how such an objective could be attained, does not appeal to my reason. I may be wrong in that, and I may be censured for the speech which I am now making. Very well, let the censure come. I am not going to curb my intelligence for fear of censure from anybody, and I say that is not my understanding of playing even the party game. It is censuring the government for not doing that which was an impossibility in the time allotted to it.
I turn to the speech of the hon. member for Lisgar to make sure that in the summary I have given of the amendment I have not misinterpreted his ideas. He says in one part of his speech that there are one or two things to which he intends to refer, that might be considered as being of a more constructive nature. I want to mention these things of a more constructive nature in order that I may be perfectly fair to my hon. friend and also fair to myself, because if we were to read these constructive things into his motion, I would have to judge as to whether or not I would be warranted in voting for his amendment considered in the light of his remarks made in the discussion of it.
With regard to these constructive suggestions, the first is a protest that a certain Mr. Wilson was to be withdrawn from Great Britain as our agricultural representative. That docs not impress me as being a constructive economic policy. I cannot conceive that the price of wheat or the market for wheat would be very materially altered by keeping either Mr. Wilson or any other gentleman where he is, although I have no doubt the gentleman referred to is doing good service. But, as it happens, my hon. friend was immediately assured by the Prime Minister that the vote in this respect was larger than last year and that the office referred to would be continued, so that that constructive idea may be set aside.
The next constructive idea is the reduction of internal freight rates. This, of course, is not a new question. There is a real problem to be solved by some government in regard to internal freight rates, but I cannot help saying that that has not developed since this government was elected. That question is not one year old; it has been a Canadian problem for a long time, and I am amazed that my hon. friend did not move this during the last session of the last iparliament; that he did not use his influence when the party to which he belongs was in power; .that he did
Agricultural Conditions

not during the last five, six, or seven years make a plea that this be corrected. But why we should move it now as a vote of no confidence in a government that has been in power nine months, when other governments might have fixed it a generation ago, I am not clear, neither do I regard this suggestion as being particularly constructive. I am informed by some hon. gentlemen who pretend to know law. that the question is scarcely one for parliament at all; that at. least it is doubtful whether it is, and that there exists machinery which has been set up for the purpose of regulating these freight rates and which should be set in motion to correct the grievance referred to by my hon. friend.
The last constructive suggestion is the consideration of the meat problem, a suggestion which was made first in the house so far as I know, by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), that the government should take action in certain experimental ways in regard to packing and the live stock business generally. I understand the government, as the Minister of Agriculture has just said, have been working towards this end and that they intend to take action on that very point; but again my hon. friend, as the Prime Minister pointed out, should have considered this for the last eight years. We have it from his own lips that just a few years ago he was knocking his own pigs on t'he head, or should have done so, because they were a dead loss. They would be, of course, if he knocked them on the head. But even then my hon. friend said nothing about the packing plants. He moved no vote of censure of the government then in power for not taking action, and that, government was in power for many years, during which they could have been censured. I know that to reiterate this is the old political game. I do not want to play it, but I am trying to be fair to this administration. I will frankly say that I would rather enjoy voting the government out of office, if we could do it, upon an issue that mattered; but I do not think that the issue before us is a fair one.
I come to the last reason mentioned by me for refusing to vote for the amendment, and that is that I think it is unfair to the Minister of Agriculture. Personally, so far as I am concerned, I want to give him a chance. That is what he was elected for. The people of Canada decided that about nine months ago, and I do not know that they have changed their minds in the meantime. Though I have no doubt that they will some time, I have no authority to say that they have done so as yet. So I say that in all fairness the amend-
IMr. Iivine.j
ment should not have been moved at this time.
As I have already said, if next year the Minister of Agriculture shall have proved himself a failure, if there is evidence that the action or inaction of the government in regard to agriculture has been detrimental to the economic life of the country or that any policy which the government has advanced has been injurious to Canadian trade or detrimental in any other way, then I shall speak against the government perhaps with a great deal more enthusiasm than I am now speaking for it. I am not asking any favours of the government or of anybody else. I am simply trying to face this issue as squarely as I can. I frankly state, Mr. Speaker, that if I could have sat in my seat while this vote *was going on without creating an uproar I would have done so, because while I am not going to vote for the amendment, I am not particularly enthusiastic about supporting the government; but since I have been compelled, practically, by the sentiment of this assembly, to register my vote either yes or no, I feel bound to say why I go over the line a little bit to say no with respect to this particular amendment.
In conclusion, in view of the universal depression to which every member who has spoken has made reference and recognizing that this depression has its roots in causes that extend far back, and which have produced results over a period of years; in view also of the nature of the policies to be evolved to meet the situation, which necessarily require time, I think it is not fair to censure the Minister of Agriculture before he has been given a chance to act. I frankly say that I have great confidence in him personally. I believe that he has only one object, and until I find it otherwise I shall continue to believe that. I believe that his one object is to devote himself to the Department of Agriculture, to relieve the present situation, so far as it is within the power of the government to do so and to evolve policies which, taking the long view, it is thought will be to the advantage of agriculture in the future.
