speechtext:
['I will tell the hon. gentleman in a few moments what the use of talking is, because I am not going to talk for the sake of a party or in any hope that some day this little group will be on the right of Mr. Speaker. I am going to speak on the issue as I see it, without any frills on either side of it.
Before addressing myself specifically to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown), I wish to make a reference to the speech of the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh). This afternoon the hon. gentleman went a long piece out of his way to make an attack on me because of a speech I made in this house some time ago. He did not attack the speech itself but merely an aside in that speech, w'hich made a reference to secession talk in the west. As some other hon. members have done, he attributed to me the blame for, or the honour, as the case may be, of first introducing that question in the House of Commons this session. I just wish to call the attention of the house and of the Ottawa Journal to the fact that I was not the first to mention that question in the house; the first one to mention it in the house was the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull). He quoted the ex-premier of [DOT]Saskatchewan in his reference to the matter. The next hon. member to mention it was the member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallanee), who even went so far as to hold aloft that famous "Charter of Liberty" drawn up in the province of Saskatchewan. The next hon. member to refer to the matter was the deputy speaker of the house (Mr. LaVergne). These hon. gentlemen scoffed at the idea but in my reference to it I said only that I thought perhaps the hon. gentlemen did not understand as well as they might the conditions prevailing in the west and that there might be more in the secession talk than was imagined. That remark acted as a match to the powder barrel of the Ottawa Journal and hurt the feelings of my hon. friend to my right who made a reference to it this afternoon. I trust that this will be sufficient to prove to my hon. friend that I was not the first to mention the matter in this house.
I shall now address myself to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown). In doing so I would say in all kindness that the Liberal party is always great in opposition but I am afraid that if they are not careful they will prove themselves to be so great that the country will want to keep them always in that position. The hon. member for Lisgar is one of the most respected members in this house. He is possessed of a matured and balanced judgment, is well informed on all matters pertaining to agriculture and has advanced in this chamber on many occasions very interesting views on agricultural economics. I listened to his speech on his amendment, I have since read it very carefully and I must confess that I agree with a great deal of what he said. I do not think he overstated the case in referring to the conditions prevailing in the west and I stand with him in his earnestness and sincerity to endeavour to find some means of alleviation and in looking forward to some policy to safeguard a return of normal conditions. Nevertheless, when I come to examine his amendment I do not feel so much in keeping with his thoughts. I intend to oppose that amendment, and will give my reasons for so doing.
The amendment does not make a definite, constructive proposal. It was moved as a protest against the speech of the Prime Minister. What I am about to say may not be popular in the west, or in my own riding, because of the fact that the Prime Minister's speech referred to did meet with some resentment. I agree with my hon. friend that that speech will be regarded by the western farmer as indicative of a lack of sympathy, but I believe that when the western farmer understands the relief actually given by this government he will then realize that when the Prime Minister made that speech he knew that conditions in the west were bad indeed.
The suggestion as to markets made in the last paragraph of the amendment is too vague and nebulous to warrant one's voting nonconfidence in a government which has not been in office one year, furthermore, the amendment is unfair to the Minister of Agriculture who has just taken over the responsibilities of office.
The amendment regrets that the administration has failed to implement its promises with respect to agriculture and that it has not announced any policy. I thought that the last election was singularly empty of promises so far as agriculture was concerned. That was one of the objections we had in my riding to the Conservative party; that it
Agricultural Conditions', "made no promises to agriculture but had made a great many to the other classes. It may be that in the province from which my hon. friend come such promises were made, but so far as the keeping of promises is concerned, we feel that we can deal with the government on that score at the proper time. I do not think it is fair inside of one year to expect the government to have made a very definite impression upon the economic conditions prevailing in Canada.
Speaking of agriculture specifically, I think the hon. Minister of Agriculture put his finger on the point when he referred to the fact that the conditions from which agriculture is suffering were not developed during the last nine months but had been developing during the last nine years. I do not blame the previous government for having developed these conditions because there are many reasons apart from anything the past government could have done to account for the present state of western agriculture, and in all fairness we must admit that present day conditions have not been brought, about by the advent of the present administration. As to a policy not having been announced, I think the Prime Minister stated in one of his speeches that the Minister of Agriculture would announce his policy when he brought down his estimates. I am quite prepared to give the Minister of Agriculture and the government at least one year in which to deal with agriculture and other matters of importance in Canada. I do not know what they intend to do; I do not know that we will be any better off next year than we are this year, but I owe it to my own sense of fairness to give the government that opportunity. If my hon. friend is still of the same opinion next year-he probably will be even though the government may have done something by that time-I will then stand with him in criticism of the government if it has failed to take advantage of its opportunity to do something.
The amendment next refers to the policies ol the administration restricting rather than expanding trade. I am at a loss to understand just what the hon. gentleman means by this, because in the first clause he denounces the government for not having a policy and in the next clause complains that the policy of the government is a restriction of trade. It may be that he had the belief that the general policy of the government restricted trade and no policy has been announced for agriculture. If that were the hon. gentleman's belief then the clauses would

have some meaning, but if he referred in both cases to a general policy, then there would be a direct contradiction.
The amendment then goes on to state that without the development of international trade Canadian agriculture will become increasingly paralyzed. In this regard I refer to the statement made by the previous speaker (Mr. Vallance) in answer to a question asked by the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion). The hon. minister asked the question: How is it that more wheat is being sold this year than last, to which the hon. member for South Battleford replied that it was being given away this year. I agree with him in his answer, but it was given away last year as well and in that respect he was unfair. Wheat is being sold this year at the world price just as it was sold last year on that basis, therefore both this government and the last government are in exactly the same position in relation to the price of wheat.
The amendment states that any policy brought forward with respect to agriculture should include emergency measures to meet the present crisis. According to the statement just made by the Minister of Agriculture, an emergency policy has been in force for some time. I understand that he went to Winnipeg in January last; that he met there representatives of the western provinces; that an agreement or arrangement was made which was satisfactory to the premiers of the western provinces in respect to certain relief, and that for some good reason on the part of the western provinces, the actual conditions of the agreement, so far as they had to do with the federal government, were not made public; so that would appear to settle the emergency part of the resolution with which we are dealing.
Finally, the suggestion is that adequate provision should be made for the processing of meats and the marketing of live stock, wheat, dairy, and all other agriculture products. That, of course, should be done, but I have not heard any hon. member, nor have I heard any one outside of the house, put forward a single proposal that would be calculated to bring a cent more for wheat than we are now getting. If the hon. member who moved this amendment will put forward a concrete proposal that will give even a promise of a penny more a bushel, I shall vote for it, but so far in all the speeches that have been delivered in the house this session, I have not heard a proposal that would raise the price of wheat or pork or eggs or butter or any other commodity. Indeed, this par-

Agricultural Conditions
liament would have great difficulty in altering materially the price of any one of these commodities. I think hon. gentlemen who expect, that or talk as if they expected it, know better. They know that our present system and the conditions under which we are living and operating are such that laws not passed by parliament, but laws of economic significance, determine the price of all these commodities, and that no proposal which could be made by parliament, so far as I am aware, apart from actually bonusing wheat or pegging the price, would produce the result that we desire. The government has stated very emphatically that it will not peg the price of wheat, and I am not sure that I want it to do so. I question very much the economic sense of such a proposition and I have done so ever since it was first made. I have expressed my opinion in that regard in other places than in this chamber.
But with regard to relief for farmers, the government can take action, and as regards the debt which is on the back of the farmers, which did not come last year, but which has been accumulating and accumulating for a generation due to a bad policy of finance which has been adopted by all governments and due to unrestricted interest rates and other things from which agriculture has been suffering, that burden of debt might be relieved by some arrangement which the government might make. It might be possible to fix the interest at a lower rate or to get the mortgage companies to think reasonable in regard to the situation and to cancel the interest for last year and the year before so as to give the farmers an opportunity to come back when conditions improve. The government maybe could not do that by law, but they might be able to do it by consultation and advice. Apart from that I do not believe any suggestion has been made that would guarantee to the farmers even a hope of getting a higher price for wheat.
While that is so, we have here a motion of no confidence moved against a government that is really sitting now in its first session, because it has not raised the price of wheat or found a better market for wheat or other things. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I am very anxious to find a better market for the western farmers; I am very anxious to see them get more for their wheat, and I say again if any hon. gentleman on this or the other side of the house will put forward an idea that will give a hope of doing that, I shall readily vote for it, no matter what party he belongs to. But in the first session of a government that has not
been in power one year, to move a vote of no confidence in them for not getting a better market and to do this without making a suggestion of how such an objective could be attained, does not appeal to my reason. I may be wrong in that, and I may be censured for the speech which I am now making. Very well, let the censure come. I am not going to curb my intelligence for fear of censure from anybody, and I say that is not my understanding of playing even the party game. It is censuring the government for not doing that which was an impossibility in the time allotted to it.
I turn to the speech of the hon. member for Lisgar to make sure that in the summary I have given of the amendment I have not misinterpreted his ideas. He says in one part of his speech that there are one or two things to which he intends to refer, that might be considered as being of a more constructive nature. I want to mention these things of a more constructive nature in order that I may be perfectly fair to my hon. friend and also fair to myself, because if we were to read these constructive things into his motion, I would have to judge as to whether or not I would be warranted in voting for his amendment considered in the light of his remarks made in the discussion of it.
With regard to these constructive suggestions, the first is a protest that a certain Mr. Wilson was to be withdrawn from Great Britain as our agricultural representative. That docs not impress me as being a constructive economic policy. I cannot conceive that the price of wheat or the market for wheat would be very materially altered by keeping either Mr. Wilson or any other gentleman where he is, although I have no doubt the gentleman referred to is doing good service. But, as it happens, my hon. friend was immediately assured by the Prime Minister that the vote in this respect was larger than last year and that the office referred to would be continued, so that that constructive idea may be set aside.
The next constructive idea is the reduction of internal freight rates. This, of course, is not a new question. There is a real problem to be solved by some government in regard to internal freight rates, but I cannot help saying that that has not developed since this government was elected. That question is not one year old; it has been a Canadian problem for a long time, and I am amazed that my hon. friend did not move this during the last session of the last iparliament; that he did not use his influence when the party to which he belongs was in power; .that he did
Agricultural Conditions", "not during the last five, six, or seven years make a plea that this be corrected. But why we should move it now as a vote of no confidence in a government that has been in power nine months, when other governments might have fixed it a generation ago, I am not clear, neither do I regard this suggestion as being particularly constructive. I am informed by some hon. gentlemen who pretend to know law. that the question is scarcely one for parliament at all; that at. least it is doubtful whether it is, and that there exists machinery which has been set up for the purpose of regulating these freight rates and which should be set in motion to correct the grievance referred to by my hon. friend.
The last constructive suggestion is the consideration of the meat problem, a suggestion which was made first in the house so far as I know, by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), that the government should take action in certain experimental ways in regard to packing and the live stock business generally. I understand the government, as the Minister of Agriculture has just said, have been working towards this end and that they intend to take action on that very point; but again my hon. friend, as the Prime Minister pointed out, should have considered this for the last eight years. We have it from his own lips that just a few years ago he was knocking his own pigs on t'he head, or should have done so, because they were a dead loss. They would be, of course, if he knocked them on the head. But even then my hon. friend said nothing about the packing plants. He moved no vote of censure of the government then in power for not taking action, and that, government was in power for many years, during which they could have been censured. I know that to reiterate this is the old political game. I do not want to play it, but I am trying to be fair to this administration. I will frankly say that I would rather enjoy voting the government out of office, if we could do it, upon an issue that mattered; but I do not think that the issue before us is a fair one.
I come to the last reason mentioned by me for refusing to vote for the amendment, and that is that I think it is unfair to the Minister of Agriculture. Personally, so far as I am concerned, I want to give him a chance. That is what he was elected for. The people of Canada decided that about nine months ago, and I do not know that they have changed their minds in the meantime. Though I have no doubt that they will some time, I have no authority to say that they have done so as yet. So I say that in all fairness the amend-
IMr. Iivine.j
ment should not have been moved at this time.
As I have already said, if next year the Minister of Agriculture shall have proved himself a failure, if there is evidence that the action or inaction of the government in regard to agriculture has been detrimental to the economic life of the country or that any policy which the government has advanced has been injurious to Canadian trade or detrimental in any other way, then I shall speak against the government perhaps with a great deal more enthusiasm than I am now speaking for it. I am not asking any favours of the government or of anybody else. I am simply trying to face this issue as squarely as I can. I frankly state, Mr. Speaker, that if I could have sat in my seat while this vote *was going on without creating an uproar I would have done so, because while I am not going to vote for the amendment, I am not particularly enthusiastic about supporting the government; but since I have been compelled, practically, by the sentiment of this assembly, to register my vote either yes or no, I feel bound to say why I go over the line a little bit to say no with respect to this particular amendment.
In conclusion, in view of the universal depression to which every member who has spoken has made reference and recognizing that this depression has its roots in causes that extend far back, and which have produced results over a period of years; in view also of the nature of the policies to be evolved to meet the situation, which necessarily require time, I think it is not fair to censure the Minister of Agriculture before he has been given a chance to act. I frankly say that I have great confidence in him personally. I believe that he has only one object, and until I find it otherwise I shall continue to believe that. I believe that his one object is to devote himself to the Department of Agriculture, to relieve the present situation, so far as it is within the power of the government to do so and to evolve policies which, taking the long view, it is thought will be to the advantage of agriculture in the future."]

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when the New Brunswick items were before the committee last, it was understood that while they were adopted in general I would have the privilege when they were brought up again to deal with .certain matters in respect to which I had asked the production of correspondence. I drew the attention of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart), after this correspondence had been tabled, to the fact that some of it was lacking. The next day he was kind enough to produce what was supposed to be all the correspondence and documents in connection with the undertaking. Now, I am not going to try to prevent the adoption of these items because of the fact that, notwithstanding a second attempt has been made to produce the correspondence and documents, the file is still incomplete. There is nothing on the file produced to show the details of the account rendered for the services of the legal representative of the Department of Justice. The Minister of Public Works can well say that that correspondence is in the Department of Justice, but when a member asks for all the correspondence it is the duty of each department having to do with the matter to produce that correspondence. I refer to this more

for the purpose of reminding the committee that a great deal of dissatisfaction was expressed by my hon. friends opposite during the last session of parliament in 1930, because of some of the files then produced by myself as Postmaster Genera! not being complete, it being insinuated that those files had been rendered incomplete for a certain purpose. Although I attempted to justify myself on that occasion by showing that the incomplete part of the file was the part which was handled by the 'Civil Service Commission, still hon. members opposite insisted that the items in my department should not pass until the entire file was produced. While I am anxious, Mr. Chairman, to see the account as rendered by the representative of the Department of Justice, I do not intend at this moment to insist any further upon its production, but to ask the Minister of Public Works if he will be kind enough to see that the Justice department produce to him a detailed statement of that account and allow me to have a copy.
I wish to direct the attention of the committee to the proposed construction of a wharf at Little Shippigan, Gloucester county. I do not wish to delay the passage of these items, but I ask for the production of that account because I understand from the correspondence which is here that a cheque for fifty dollars was issued for the service of the gentleman in question. I understand that, on the production of deeds, two cheques were issued for land appropriated by the department for the construction of this wharf. These cheques were issued to two gentlemen, a Mr. Brown and a Mr. Brune; one for twenty dollars to Mr. Brune and the other, for fifty dollars, to Mr. Brown. I understand that these cheques were issued jointly, the first to Mr. Brown and Mr. A. M. Robi-chaud, the solicitor, and the second to Mr. Brune and Mr. Robichaud, the solicitor. I want to know why these cheques were issued jointly to the solicitor of the Department of Justice and the owner of the land. It may be the practice; I do not know. If it is the practice, I have no fault to find. But I wish to see the detailed statement of this account. And I wish, further, to protest against an expenditure of fifty dollars for obtaining land worth seventy.
While I am on the question of the proposed construction of a wharf at Little Shippigan, I see by the correspondence that on August 21, 1930, the Minister of Public Works recommended to council that the tender of C. L. Comeau be accepted; and he further recommended that an amount of
816,000	additional be placed in the estimates this year for the termination of that work

Sup-ply-Harbours and Rivers-N.B.
and to complete the contract. The tender, I believe, was in the vicinity of $26,000. Last year we voted $10,000 knowing that it would cost betwen $26,000 and $30,000, and that $10,000 was voted for the purpose of calling for tenders to have the work proceeded with. The minister recommended on August 21 that the tender of Mr. Comeau should be accepted and afterwards the recommendation was withdrawn; at least, it was not accepted by council. I should like the minister to explain this. He does attempt to give an explanation at page 16 of the correspondence submitted. In a letter to the reverend father in charge of the parish of Little Shippigan he states, at page 16 of the correspondence:
In view of the falling revenues of the government and the increased expenditures, including a special vote of $20,000,000 passed at the recent session of parliament for the relief of unemployment, it has been deemed inadvisable in the public interest to proceed with this work at the present time.
With reference to that $20,000,000, we had a statement from the Prime Minister in September as to why' this money could be used for such purposes; and to my mind this letter of November 13, 1930, in which the statement is made that in view of the falling revenues and the voting of this $20,000,000, it was considered inexpedient to go on with the work, is not a sufficient excuse. The minister at that time was in possession of information which he had a perfect right to accept as well founded, coming as it did from the parish priest of that district, and in view of a conversation with myself in regard to the unemployment situation at that particular point. And if the $20,000 000 voted by parliament could not have been expended in that way, then I claim that the work could have been proceeded with under that vote for the relief of unemployment in the district.
That district is perhaps one of the hardest hit of any section in Canada so far as unemployment is concerned. The people living on Miscou island are not an agricultural class; the island is not fitted for agriculture. They raise some very small crops, it is true, potatoes and hay. But they are fishermen; they earn their living by fishing. Last fall, however, fishing failed and these people were practically on the verge of starvation. That was represented to the minister and he had every reason to believe that the representations were correct. Yet in the face of that, refusal was given to relieve the situation as it existed at that time.
Leaving aside altogether for the moment the question of unemployment relief in that
section, and coming down to the real merits of the case, I wish to say to the minister that there is no section of the maritime provinces where the construction of a work of that kind is so necessary. These are hardy fishermen who risk their lives every day, and they have been asking for some time past for this construction. They have asked for it under previous Conservative governments; they have asked for it under previous Liberal governments; and it was only last year that I was enabled in their behalf to have this amount placed in the estimates to give them the needed protection. And there is no doubt about it that it is absolutely needed. Under the circumstances I would appeal once more to the Minister of Public Works and, as well, to the Prime Minister in his capacity as Minister of Finance; because I realize, from my experience in council, that after all the Minister of Finance has a great deal to say in matters of this kind. I appeal to both of these hon. gentlemen to see that something is placed in the supplementary estimates in order that this work may be carried on.
A tender has been received, if I mistake not, five or six thousand dollars under the estimate placed upon the work by the engineers; and, even under present circumstances, if the contract were offered to-day to the person who tendered at that time at the figure he gave, I believe, although I have no authority to speak in his behalf, that he would accept the contract at that figure.
If the vote is placed in the supplementary estimates this year it will serve two purposes. There is still unemployment in that district, and these people will not succeed in their fishing very much better this year than last year. The money would therefore relieve the situation in that section of the country. The people there are isolated; they are living on an island far from the mainland. They have no communication except by water, and with the freezing up of the bay they are unable, for four or five weeks in the fall and three or four weeks in the spring, to communicate with the mainland at all except by telephone. This work would relieve unemployment in this district because the contractor could begin work towards the fall of the year at the very time when it is necessary to provide relief. I do not desire to take i:p too much time of the committee, but let me appeal once more to the Minister of Public Works and to the Minister of Finance and direct their attention to the absolute necessity of the carrying on of this work.
Hon. H. A. STEWART (Minister of Public Works)Mr. Chairman, in reply to the

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext: With regard to his suggestion that the cheques issued for two small parcels of land should not have been made payable to the agent of the Department of Justice and to the owner of the land, I may say that that is the regular procedure.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
I said it was the practice.
fMr. H. A. Stewart.]

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
The reason is
quite evident; until the agent is satisfied that everything has been furnished he has control of the cheques. I know nothing regarding the charges, because they are settled and taxed by the Department of Justice. Let me suggest in all sincerity to my hon. friend that this agent dealt with the title to the two parcels of land. It is true that the consideration for the transfer of these two parcels is small, and although he has correctly stated the amount, I think on reflection he will agree with me that very often there is just as much work involved in searching the title of a small parcel of land as there is in searching the title of even a hundred or a thousand acres as long as the title comes down through the one chain. In this case there were two parcels the titles of which had to be searched. As I have said, the Department of Justice deals with these matters, and I will obtain the information from that source. As to why this work was not proceeded with, I think the correspondence discloses the reasons. I cannot go any further than that.
I know my hon. friend is very much interested in the work at Little Shippigan. During the short session he spoke to me about this matter and impressed upon me the importance and desirability of proceeding with the work. We were faced with the fact that an appropriation of $10,000 had been made, with a considerably larger expenditure being involved. The conclusion arrived at was that we were not in a position to do this work this year in view of the larger amount involved. I would point out to my hon. friend that a very large work is being proceeded with in his constituency at Tracadie. The department was of the opinion that this construction would afford the greatest measure of relief for unemployment, and therefore selected that work as the one which we would prosecute. The expenditure involved will amount to about $160,000 more, but notwithstanding that it was thought that as the work could be carried on continuously it would afford the greatest measure of relief.
With reference to my hon. friend's last request, that consideration be given to this matter in the supplementary estimates, all I can say is that I shall certainly give it consideration and I hope we will both live long enough to see this work completed at Little Shippigan.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AGRICULTURAL CONDITIONS   CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE AND AMENDMENT OF MR. BROWN
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have very little more to say in regard to this matter, but I do not like to hear the minister give as a reason for delaying the work-I hope it is only delayed

the fact that considerable

Business oj the House
work was being parried on at Tiracadie harbour. This work was commenced in 1929 when some three or four thousands dollars was expended in protecting the beach to which the' channel is to be dredged. The dredge boat went in during the fall of 1929 and worked all last summer. This work has been under contemplation for some four or five years and while I am pleased to see an item to complete it I cannot accept that as sufficient reason for not going on with the -work at Little Shippigan. Other works in Gloucester county which were absolutely necessary were thrown out. There was the Little Shippigan work; there was the extension on the Young wharf for which tenders were called for and held up for quite a long time before it was decided not to continue with the work; there was the dredging at St. Simon which was included in the program of $650,000 voted last year for dredging generally in the maritime provinces; there was the dredging at Lower Caraquet which was absolutely necessary and which was included in the general program; there was the dredging of the upper channel leading to Shippigan gully through which 250 or 350 fishing vessels pass twice a week, and there was the dredging in the inner channel of the gully in Shippigan harbour, which was to be straightened out, as well as the removal of the sandbanks outside and inside of the gully. These items which have been thrown aside, if gone on with, would have considerably relieved unemployment in that section of the county, and I feel that an injustice has been lone to the county which I have the honour to represent. I may be wrong; I do not desire to impute any motive to the minister or to the government, but I think they perhaps sought the information in wrong places and decided upon information which, to my mind, was not correct. The minister, however, has stated that he will consider the request 1 made.
There is one item in regard to which I should like to have a little explanation. I think there is an item of $491.84 in the expenditure on that wharf. Would the minister please tell me what that includes? The work has not been carried on, and I should like to know what brought about this expenditure of $491.84.

May I ask
my right hon. friend whether he understands the government will be free to go into Trade and Commerce estimates to-morrow if they wish to do so?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: EFFECT OF SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 FOR THURSDAY, MAY 7
speechtext: My understanding is that we cannot take up the estimates of any new department to-morrow beyond those of Trade and Commerce. External Affairs, and Public Works, and that only one External Affairs item will be taken up namely that respecting the League of Nations, after which we shall take up Trade and Commerce. If we do not decide to continue until we finish that, then we shall take up an item on Public Works, the estimates of which are nearly all through.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: EFFECT OF SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 FOR THURSDAY, MAY 7
speechtext:
I do not think my right hon. friend is entitled to proceed with Trade and Commerce estimates tomorrow. I shall read the resolution under which we proceeded to-day. It is to be found in the Votes and Proceedings of May 6, as follows:
That the debate on the motion of the Minister of Finance that "Mr. Speaker do now
13S0
Business oj the House

leave the chair for the house to resolve itself again into committee of supply" and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Brown, be resumed on Thursday, May 7th, instant, and that standing order 28 be suspended on that day in relation thereto.
After debate thereon, the question being put on the said motion, it was agreed to.
The suspension therefore of standing order 28 is applicable only to to-day, May 7; it does not apply to to-morrow. Standing order 28 reads:
On Thursdays and Fridays when the order of the day is called for the house to go into committee of supply, or of ways and means, Mr. Speaker shall leave the chair without putting any question, provided that, except by the unanimous consent of the house, the estimates of each department shall be first taken up on a day other than Thursday or Friday.
The house has given unanimous consent to take up what we have done to-day with respect to to-day, but it has not given unanimous consent to take up the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce on a Friday or on any subsequent Thursday without having them taken up in the regular way in the first instance.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: EFFECT OF SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 FOR THURSDAY, MAY 7
speechtext: We cannot reprobate and approbate at the same time, I think Lord Eldon-once said. What has happened is that we have made to-day a Tuesday for the purpose of going into supply, and Trade and Commerce is the item which we have considered, which we could not have considered otherwise than by consent of the house. It having been so considered and the house having further consented that External Affairs be taken up to enable the hon. member for Yegreville to speak about a particular matter, my submission is that the house has now before it three supply items: Public Works, Trade and Commerce, and External Affairs, and that having agreed to take up but one item in External Affairs to-morrow; we may go on with Trade and Commerce, because that item is now properly before the committee by the consent of the house. It could not be otherwise.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: EFFECT OF SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 FOR THURSDAY, MAY 7
speechtext:
The consent
of the house was given to the taking of the item for to-day, but standing order 28 is still applicable, and while we are only too anxious to oblige the government in the matter of the expedition of its business, we must not, by giving our consent here and there, be prejudiced as respects our position in other particulars. I am quite prepared to leave the matter to Mr. Speaker to decide, but I submit that the resolution under which we proceeded to-day to consider estimates is applicable only 
to the day of May 7; that apart from that, standing order 28 is applicable for the rest of the session, indeed is applicable to the session as a whole, and that by giving consent to take up a particular estimate to-day, we have not waived the right we have under standing order 28 to refuse to give consent to taking up the estimates of any department that has not been gone into on a Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: EFFECT OF SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 FOR THURSDAY, MAY 7
speechtext:
I shall appeal from that
ruling.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: EFFECT OF SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 FOR THURSDAY, MAY 7
speechtext:
And the leader of the
opposition has signified his willingness to give unanimous consent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: EFFECT OF SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 FOR THURSDAY, MAY 7
speechtext: It is needless to say that I do not agree with that ruling, but the house can appeal from it. As it is eleven o'clock I have nothing further to say at the moment.

maintopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE
subtopic: EFFECT OF SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDER 28 FOR THURSDAY, MAY 7
speechtext: And I may say lhat the opposition will support the ruling of His Honour the Speaker.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, May 8, 1931
